title: Individual Project — A Bayesian GLMM on Your Own Data
text:
The project carries most of the course credits: an individual project with data material selected by the student, presented orally and in writing. The syllabus describes the intended complexity as a mixed model. It is where every module comes together: a model and priors you can defend (Modules 1–2, 6), MCMC that has converged (3), checks that the model fits (4), and a hierarchical structure (5).
This page answers the first question (can you use the European Social Survey?), then walks through the analysis in ten steps. Each step has a status control (Not started / In progress / Done) that is saved in your browser and summarised on the dashboard. The steps link back to the module sections they rely on.

title: Individual Project — A Bayesian GLMM on Your Own Data
section: Can you use the European Social Survey?
text:
Can you use the European Social Survey?
Very likely yes, and it is a good fit, for three reasons:

It is “data material selected by the student”. ESS data are free for non-commercial use, including study and teaching, after registering at ess.sikt.no.
It has natural hierarchical structure: respondents within regions, within countries, within survey rounds. That is exactly the “mixed model” level of complexity the syllabus asks for.
It has health outcomes, fitting a course in the Institute of Medicine: self-rated health (health, 1 = very good … 5 = very bad), hampered by illness (hlthhmp), and in some rounds smoking, alcohol, height and weight.

Things to settle early:

Confirm with the teacher that a survey dataset from outside health care is acceptable for your project. A short message with your research question and planned model is enough.
Conditions of use. You may not redistribute the data: keep the .sav files out of public repositories (including a public GitHub repo for your report). Cite each round and edition you use; the ESS website gives the exact citation with a DOI.
Survey weights. ESS provides design, post-stratification (pspwght) and analysis (anweight) weights. A Bayesian model does not use them automatically. Common options: (a) adjust for the variables the weights are built from (age, gender, education, region) and state that you model conditional on them; (b) mention multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) as the model-based Bayesian route to population estimates. brms’s weights() treats weights as frequency weights and changes the effective sample size, so do not use it without discussing that. Whatever you choose, say so in the limitations.
Few groups. Sweden has only 8 NUTS2 regions. A between-region SD estimated from 8 groups depends on its hyperprior, so a hyperprior sensitivity analysis becomes part of your results (Task 5.5). If you want more groups, download several countries and use (1 | country).

Change the file path on line 20. Tested on the Swedish all-rounds file (9,348 respondents after cleaning): the whole script ran in about 11 minutes on a 4-core laptop, with every R-hat ≤ 1.01 and bulk ESS above 900. Even with adapt_delta = 0.95, one divergent transition out of 4,000 remained. The round-level SD is estimated close to zero with only six rounds, which creates a funnel-shaped posterior; Step 5 below says how to handle that. No results from the ESS data are shown on this public site.
It is a starting point, not your project: replace the question, justify the priors in your own words, and add the checks and sensitivity analyses your question needs.

section: Step 2 · Data: selection, cleaning, missing values
text:
Step 2 · Data: selection, cleaning, missing values

Choose rounds and respondents (for example rounds 5–11, age 18+). Report the numbers at each exclusion step.
ESS missing codes (refusal, don’t know, not applicable: 7/8/9, 77/88/99, …) become NA when read with haven::read_sav(). Check with table(x, useNA = "ifany").
Recode: binary outcome, age in decades centred at 50, education in 3 levels (ES-ISCED 1–2, 3–4, 5–7; code 55 “other” → NA), region harmonised to NUTS2.
Missing data: a complete-case analysis is simplest; report how many rows were dropped and discuss whether that could bias results. (brms can also impute within the model with mi(), or fit to multiply imputed datasets with brm_multiple().)
Keep the raw data out of any public repository.

section: Step 3 · Model: likelihood and structure, written out
text:
Step 3 · Model: likelihood and structure, written out
Write the model three ways, as in 5.7:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{good\_health}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i)\\
\text{logit}(p_i) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{age}_i + \beta_2 \text{age}_i^2 + \beta_3 \text{female}_i + \beta_{\text{edu}[i]} + u_{\text{region}[i]} + v_{\text{round}[i]}\\
u_j &\sim N(0, \tau_\text{region}^2), \qquad v_k \sim N(0, \tau_\text{round}^2)
\end{aligned}\]
brms: good_health ~ age10 + I(age10^2) + female + edu_level + (1 | region2) + (1 | round). In words: each region and each survey round has its own baseline, drawn from a common distribution; age, sex and education shift everyone’s log-odds by the same amount.
Justify each choice: why this likelihood, why these covariates (confounders, precision), why random rather than fixed effects for region and round, why (or why not) varying slopes.

section: Step 4 · Priors and a prior predictive check
text:
Step 4 · Priors and a prior predictive check

List every parameter that needs a prior: get_prior(formula, data, family).
Choose weakly informative priors on a sensible scale (6.4) and write a sentence of justification for each. For example: “normal(0, 1) on log odds ratios: an odds ratio above 7 for a one-decade age difference or between education levels is implausible.”
Fit with sample_prior = "only" and check the implied share with good health overall and by age (6.2). Put one prior predictive plot in the report.

title: Individual Project — A Bayesian GLMM on Your Own Data
text:
Step 5 · Fit and check convergence

4 chains, at least 2,000 iterations each; seed = for reproducibility; file = to save the fit.
Report: R-hat (all < 1.01), bulk and tail ESS (> 400; ≥ 1,000 for the parameters you report), zero divergent transitions, and trace plots for the key parameters (3.8, 3.9, 3.10).
Divergences in a GLMM: first increase adapt_delta to 0.95 or 0.99; if they persist, look at the group-level SD priors. They typically appear when a group-level SD is close to zero (few groups, little between-group variation): the posterior of the group effects then has a funnel shape. A single divergence out of 4,000 is usually harmless, but report it and show that the estimates do not change with adapt_delta = 0.99.
Individual-level Bernoulli models with 10,000+ rows take minutes. For a faster first pass, you can aggregate to binomial counts per combination of the categorical covariates: successes | trials(n) ~ .... The posterior is identical when all covariates are categorical.

Step 8 · Sensitivity analysis
Refit the main model with different priors for the group-level SDs (e.g. exponential(1) vs exponential(5) vs half-Student-t) and, if relevant, for the key coefficient (6.5). With 8 regions the SD prior matters: show how τ, the MOR and the region-specific estimates change. Also consider a model choice: complete-case vs a sensitivity check on missing data, or with vs without adjusting for a debatable covariate.

text:
Step 10 · Write-up and presentation
A structure that follows the workflow:

Question and estimand.
Data: source and citation, rounds, exclusions with counts, recoding, missing data.
Model: the three representations from Step 3; priors with justification; the prior predictive check.
Computation: software versions (packageVersion("brms")), chains, iterations, diagnostics.
Model checking and comparison: PPCs, LOO table.
Results: estimands with credible intervals, in words (“the posterior probability that … is 0.93”).
Sensitivity: priors and model choices.
Discussion: limitations (weights and representativeness, few regions, cross-sectional data and no causal claims, missing data), what changed during the analysis and why (6.3), and the role of subjective choices (6.8).

For the oral presentation: one slide each for question, data, model (formula + one sentence), checks (one PPC plot), main result (one figure), sensitivity, limitations. Be ready to explain why each prior and why partial pooling.






NoteCommon mistakes in Bayesian GLMM projects






Interpreting the summary before checking diagnostics.
Reporting sd(Intercept) on the log-odds scale without translating it (MOR, or probabilities for regions).
Calling the 95% interval a confidence interval, or interpreting it as one.
Leaving brms default priors without saying what they are.
Showing only pp_check(fit) for a binary outcome: the default density plot says almost nothing there. Use stat and stat_grouped.
Treating region estimates from a model with 8 regions as precise, without a hyperprior sensitivity analysis.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
Many datasets consist of groups: patients in hospitals, respondents in regions, repeated measurements in patients, studies in a meta-analysis. You then need a parameter per group, and the number of parameters grows with the data. What prior should 200 hospital-specific parameters get? Using the same prior for all of them already says they are similar. A hierarchical model makes that similarity explicit and learns from the data how similar they are.
The model has two levels. Each group’s parameter is drawn from a common population distribution, say \(N(\mu, \tau^2)\), and \(\mu\) and \(\tau\) get priors of their own (hyperpriors). This is the “chicken and egg” of the notes: the group estimates need the population distribution as their prior, and the population distribution is estimated from the groups. The hierarchical model estimates both at once.
The result is partial pooling: each group’s estimate is a compromise between its own data and the population mean, exactly the shrinkage of Module 2. Groups with little data are pulled strongly towards the mean; groups with a lot of data mostly keep their own estimate. Complete pooling (all groups identical) and no pooling (groups unrelated) are the two extremes, reached when \(\tau \to 0\) or \(\tau \to \infty\).
This is a generalised linear mixed model (GLMM), the model class of your individual project. In brms it is one extra term in the formula: (1 | hospital).

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
5.1 Why hierarchical models?

The number of parameters grows with the data. One term per child, hospital or study. Flat priors for each give noisy, unstable estimates (and infinite ones for a group where everyone had the outcome).
Similar-yet-distinct groups. Hospitals are not identical (complete pooling is wrong) but not unrelated either (no pooling throws away information).
Something is better than nothing. From Module 1: a good prior plus one observation beats a flat prior plus one observation. For a small group, the other groups provide that prior.
Prediction for new groups needs a distribution of group effects; a model with a separate fixed parameter per group has no such distribution.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
5.3 The hyperprior
The prior on \(\tau\) decides how much pooling the model does a priori; the data update it. Choosing it is harder than choosing a prior for a mean, because intuition about SDs of log-odds is weak.

Common choices: exponential(1) (mean 1), half-normal normal(0, 1) (brms truncates it at 0 for class sd), half Student-t student_t(3, 0, 2.5) (the brms default).
Think on the scale of the linear predictor. On the log-odds scale, \(\tau = 1\) means that hospitals one SD apart differ by an odds ratio of \(e^{1} \approx 2.7\), and the middle 95% of hospitals span an odds-ratio range of \(e^{4} \approx 55\). That is a lot of variation; \(\tau\) around 0.2–0.5 is more typical.
With few groups the hyperprior matters. Five or six groups carry little information about \(\tau\) (you estimate an SD from five numbers). With 50 groups the data dominate. Task 5.5 shows this.
A flat prior on \(\tau\) is possible (the notes do it in the meta-analysis) but can give improper posteriors or divergences; brms may need adapt_delta near 1.

Empirical Bayes estimates \(\tau\) first and then plugs it in as if known. The notes’ comparison: it “purchases a duck and hopes for chicken eggs”. It uses the data twice and ignores the uncertainty in \(\tau\), so intervals are too narrow.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
5.4 How much shrinkage?
For a normal hierarchical model with known group standard errors \(s_j\) (the building block of meta-analysis):
\[\hat\theta_j = \frac{\bar y_j / s_j^2 + \mu / \tau^2}{1/s_j^2 + 1/\tau^2} = \bar y_j - \underbrace{\frac{s_j^2}{s_j^2 + \tau^2}}_{\text{shrinkage factor } B_j}\,(\bar y_j - \mu).\]
The shrinkage factor \(B_j\) is large when the group’s own estimate is noisy (\(s_j\) large: few observations) or the groups are similar (\(\tau\) small). This is the Module 2 formula, with the population distribution playing the role of the prior.
Consequences:

Extreme raw estimates usually come from small groups (noise), and they move most. Ranking hospitals on raw rates rewards and punishes small hospitals by chance.
Differences between groups shrink, so credible intervals for differences more often include zero. Gelman, Hill and Yajima (2012) proposed partial pooling as an alternative to multiple-comparison corrections.
Group estimates are biased towards the mean but have lower total error: see 5.9.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
5.8 Varying slopes and correlated effects
With repeated measurements, patients differ in their level and in their change over time:
\[y_{it} \sim N\big(\beta_0 + u_{0i} + (\beta_1 + u_{1i})\,t,\ \sigma^2\big), \qquad \begin{pmatrix} u_{0i} \\ u_{1i}\end{pmatrix} \sim N\left(\mathbf 0, \begin{pmatrix}\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1 \\ \rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2\end{pmatrix}\right)\]
brms: y ~ t + (1 + t | patient). Priors: class = "sd" for \(\tau_0, \tau_1\); class = "cor" with lkj(2) for the correlation matrix (LKJ(1) is uniform over correlations; larger values favour correlations near 0). brms builds the covariance prior from separate SD and correlation priors, which is easier than an inverse-Wishart prior.

A negative \(\rho\): patients who start high tend to fall faster (regression to the mean, or a treatment that helps most where there is most to gain).
Group-specific effects of a treatment, (1 + treat | village), let the treatment effect differ between groups: heterogeneous effects.
Varying slopes need enough observations per group and enough groups; otherwise \(\tau_1\) and \(\rho\) are poorly identified and you get divergences.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
5.9 The bias–variance trade-off
\[\text{MSE} = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}.\]

No pooling: unbiased per group, high variance (especially small groups).
Complete pooling: low variance, biased for every group that is not average.
Partial pooling: a little bias towards the mean, much less variance. Usually the lowest total error, which is why hierarchical models tend to predict better.

The hyperprior governs the trade-off: all prior mass at \(\tau = 0\) gives complete pooling, \(\tau = \infty\) gives no pooling. The classical analogue is penalised regression (ridge, LASSO), where a tuning parameter is chosen by cross-validation; in the hierarchical model \(\tau\) is estimated along with everything else. The same idea of “overfit, then regularise” underlies splines and GAMMs (s(x) in brms).

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage

5.10 Random-effects meta-analysis
A meta-analysis is a hierarchical model with studies as groups:









Fixed effect (“common effect”)
Random effects




Assumes
every study estimates the same effect
study effects \(\theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)\)


brms (individual data, binary outcome)
deaths \| trials(n) ~ 0 + study + treat
deaths \| trials(n) ~ 0 + study + treat + (0 + treat \| study)


Uncertainty about \(\mu\)
smaller

(0 + study gives each study its own baseline risk without assuming a distribution for it.)
Lessons from the notes’ magnesium example (where small trials suggested a large benefit that a huge later trial did not confirm):

The random-effects estimate is less precise, and its centre can differ from the fixed-effect estimate: small studies get relatively more weight.
With few studies, both the prior on the overall effect and the hyperprior on \(\tau\) change the conclusion. A sceptical prior on the effect (e.g. normal(0, 0.5) on the log odds ratio) is a legitimate sensitivity analysis.
Publication bias and study selection are outside the model: no prior fixes a biased set of studies.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
5.11 Ranking groups
“Which hospital is best?” Rank the groups within every posterior draw, then summarise the ranks:
share_draws <- posterior_linpred(fit, transform = TRUE)    # draws x groups
rank_draws  <- t(apply(-share_draws, 1, rank))             # rank 1 = highest share
colMeans(rank_draws)                                       # posterior mean rank
apply(rank_draws, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))    # 95% interval for each rank
colMeans(rank_draws <= 3)                                  # P(in the top 3)
Rank intervals are typically very wide: most groups could be anywhere from near the top to near the bottom. League tables based on point estimates hide this.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
section: When to use a hierarchical model
text:
When to use a hierarchical model

Clustered or repeated data: patients in hospitals, pupils in schools, measurements in patients, respondents in regions and survey rounds.
Many related parameters: subgroup effects, item difficulties, study effects in a meta-analysis.
Small groups that need to borrow strength, or predictions for groups not in the data.
As a regulariser when there are many coefficients of the same kind.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
Limitations

The normal distribution of group effects is an assumption. It is hard to check, because the estimates are themselves shrunk towards normality.
Few groups (fewer than about 5–10) carry little information on \(\tau\); results then depend on the hyperprior.
Group effects are assumed independent of the covariates. If a group-level confounder correlates with \(x\), the estimate of \(x\)’s effect can be biased; consider adding group means of \(x\) as covariates.
Complex random-effect structures converge slowly and cause divergences; a non-centred parameterisation (brms uses one by default) and tighter priors help.
LOO for hierarchical models answers “new observation in an existing group”. For new groups, use grouped k-fold CV (4.8).

Task 5.1 · Three ways to pool: HbA1c at target in 15 clinics
set.seed(530)
clinics <- data.frame(
  clinic     = LETTERS[1:15],
  n_patients = c(8, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 120, 150, 200, 250)
)
true_logodds <- rnorm(15, mean = qlogis(0.55), sd = 0.5)
clinics$at_target <- rbinom(15, size = clinics$n_patients, prob = plogis(true_logodds))

Fit the complete-pooling, no-pooling and partial-pooling models from the table in 5.2 (priors: normal(0, 1.5) on the log-odds, exponential(1) on the SD).
Make a table of the posterior mean share at target per clinic under each model.
Plot how far each clinic moves (no pooling minus partial pooling) against its number of patients.

fit_complete <- brm(at_target | trials(n_patients) ~ 1, family = binomial(),
                    prior = prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
                    data = clinics, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 530, refresh = 0)

                prior = prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"),
                data = clinics, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 530, refresh = 0)

                   prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
                             prior(exponential(1), class = "sd")),
                   data = clinics, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 530, refresh = 0)

share_partial <- colMeans(posterior_linpred(fit_partial, transform = TRUE))

                         observed = clinics$at_target / clinics$n_patients,
                         no_pooling = share_none, partial_pooling = share_partial,
                         complete_pooling = share_complete)

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
Why-questions






NoteWhy do the most extreme raw estimates usually come from the smallest groups?





Small groups have large sampling variance, so their observed rates scatter widely around their true rates. The extremes of a noisy list are mostly noise. Partial pooling pulls them back in proportion to their noise.









NoteWhy can’t the no-pooling model predict a new hospital?





It has a separate parameter for each observed hospital and no distribution connecting them. A new hospital has no parameter and nothing to draw one from. The hierarchical model supplies \(N(\mu, \tau^2)\).









NoteWhy is a hierarchical model “Bayesian” even when fitted with lme4?





The group effects get a distribution whose parameters are estimated from the data: a prior learned from the other groups. lme4 estimates μ and τ by (restricted) maximum likelihood and plugs them in, much like empirical Bayes; brms also integrates over their uncertainty.

title: Module 5 — Hierarchical Models and Shrinkage
text:
Spaced review: Modules 1–4






Note1. What does the shrinkage formula from Module 2 have in common with partial pooling?





Both pull an estimate towards a prior mean by a fraction (sampling variance)/(sampling variance + prior variance). In a hierarchical model the “prior” is the estimated population distribution. (2.3)









Note2. How would you check whether a random intercept for region is needed?





Posterior predictive check of the region means (stat_grouped by region) for the model without it, and loo_compare with and without the term; think about grouped CV if the question is about new regions. (4.3, 4.8)









Note3. A varying-slopes model gives 30 divergent transitions. First step?





Increase adapt_delta (e.g. 0.99); if they persist, tighten the priors on the SDs and correlation or simplify the random-effect structure. Divergences can bias the estimates. (3.7)

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
Conjugate priors and grids got us exact posteriors for one or two parameters. Real models have dozens or hundreds: a regression with ten covariates, a mixed model with one term per hospital. A grid is hopeless there (1,000 points per parameter and 100 parameters is \(10^{300}\) evaluations), and there is no formula. We need a way to get the posterior without ever computing the normalising integral.
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) does this. It takes a random walk through parameter space, designed so that the walk spends time in each region in proportion to its posterior probability. After a warm-up, the visited points are (dependent) draws from the posterior, and every summary from Module 1 (means, percentiles, probabilities, predictions) becomes an average over draws. The trick that avoids the integral: the algorithms only ever need ratios of the unnormalised posterior, prior × likelihood, and the unknown constant cancels in a ratio.
The price is that MCMC is only guaranteed to work eventually. In practice you must check that the chains have converged and that you have enough effectively independent draws. Trace plots, R-hat and effective sample size are the tools, and learning to read them is a syllabus outcome.
You will rarely write a sampler yourself. brms translates an R formula into a Stan program and runs the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), a form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. This page explains what happens inside, then moves to brms in RStudio.

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.1 The curse of dimensionality

Summaries are not enough. The mean and SD do not determine a distribution: a Student-t and a normal with the same mean and SD have different 95th percentiles. We want the whole posterior, including skewness and tails.
Grids grow exponentially. If one parameter needs 1,000 grid points, \(p\) parameters need \(1000^p\). Even a smarter rule with 2 points per parameter needs \(2^{195} \approx 5 \times 10^{58}\) evaluations for a model with one dummy per country.
Monte Carlo breaks the curse: its error depends on the number of (effective) draws, not directly on the number of parameters.
crumbs: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
section: 3.2 Monte Carlo and its standard error
text:
3.2 Monte Carlo and its standard error
Monte Carlo methods use random numbers but converge to fixed answers. The price is Monte Carlo error: rerun and you get a slightly different number.

Estimate it by rerunning and taking the SD of the results, or (for independent draws) by \(\text{SD}/\sqrt{S}\).
It shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{S}\): 16 times more draws for 4 times less error.
Keep it small relative to the posterior uncertainty. The notes’ rule: the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) of a posterior mean should be at least 10 times smaller than the posterior SD, preferably 100 times.

The bootstrap is a familiar Monte Carlo method (resample, refit, take the SD of the estimates). It has its own Monte Carlo error, usually ignored because 1,000+ replicates make it small. Bootstrap replicates are independent; MCMC draws are not (Section 3.10).
crumbs: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.3 Rejection sampling
To sample from a target \(f\) when you can sample from a proposal \(g\) and know \(c = \max f(x)/g(x)\):

Draw \(x \sim g\) and \(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\).
Accept \(x\) if \(u \leq f(x) / (c\, g(x))\); otherwise discard it.

Accepted draws are exact, independent draws from \(f\). The acceptance rate is \(1/c\), and \(c\) grows exponentially with the number of dimensions when \(g\) does not match \(f\). Rejection sampling is fine in one dimension and hopeless in fifty. MCMC fixes this by proposing locally, near the current point.
crumbs: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.4 Markov chains: the generic recipe
A (first-order) Markov chain generates each new value from the current one only: \(\theta^{(t)} \sim T(\theta \mid \theta^{(t-1)})\). MCMC algorithms choose the transition distribution \(T\) so that the chain’s long-run distribution is the posterior:

Start at some \(\theta^{(0)}\).
Draw \(\theta^{(t)}\) from \(T(\cdot \mid \theta^{(t-1)})\).
Repeat. After a warm-up of \(b\) iterations, treat \(\theta^{(b+1)}, \dots, \theta^{(q)}\) as draws from \(p(\theta \mid y)\).

The Markov property is a cost, not a feature: consecutive draws are autocorrelated, so 4,000 draws carry less information than 4,000 independent ones (Section 3.10). Regions with high posterior density are visited often and low-density regions rarely, but the chain can visit anywhere with non-zero density.
crumbs: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.5 The Gibbs sampler
If you can sample from each full conditional \(p(\theta_j \mid \theta_{-j}, y)\), update one parameter (or block) at a time:
\[\theta_1^{(t)} \sim p(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2^{(t-1)}, \dots, y), \quad \theta_2^{(t)} \sim p(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1^{(t)}, \theta_3^{(t-1)}, \dots, y), \quad \dots\]

Needs the conditionals in closed form, in practice conjugate priors for each parameter. This is why older software (BUGS, JAGS) encourages conjugate priors.
Moves parallel to the axes, so it is very slow when parameters are strongly correlated: each conditional is narrow and the chain creeps along a diagonal ridge.
Natural for hierarchical models, where the conditionals are simple. Multiple imputation by chained equations is essentially a Gibbs sampler.
crumbs: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.6 Metropolis and Metropolis–Hastings

Metropolis algorithm

Start at \(\theta^{(0)}\).
Propose \(\theta^* \sim J(\theta^* \mid \theta^{(t-1)})\) from a symmetric jumping distribution, e.g. \(N(\theta^{(t-1)}, \text{step}^2)\).
Compute \(r = \dfrac{p(\theta^* \mid y)}{p(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid y)} = \dfrac{p(y \mid \theta^*)\,p(\theta^*)}{p(y \mid \theta^{(t-1)})\,p(\theta^{(t-1)})}\). The normalising constant cancels.
Draw \(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). If \(u \leq r\), accept: \(\theta^{(t)} = \theta^*\). Otherwise stay: \(\theta^{(t)} = \theta^{(t-1)}\), and the old value is counted again.



Uphill moves (\(r \geq 1\)) are always accepted; downhill moves are accepted with probability \(r\). That is what makes the chain explore the whole posterior rather than climb to the mode (always accepting uphill and never downhill would be hill climbing, an optimiser).
Tuning. Tiny steps: almost everything is accepted but the chain crawls. Huge steps: almost everything is rejected and the chain sits still. An acceptance rate of roughly 0.2–0.5 works best (try it in Part B).
Metropolis–Hastings allows asymmetric proposals by using \(r = \dfrac{p(\theta^* \mid y)/J(\theta^* \mid \theta^{(t-1)})}{p(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid y)/J(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid \theta^*)}\). Plain Metropolis is the special case \(J\) symmetric.


  The chain has converged and mixes very well
  The steps are too small, so exploration is slow
  The posterior is flat, so every move is uphill
  The proposal is too wide for this posterior
  Tiny proposals land where the density is almost the same, so r ≈ 1 and nearly all are accepted, but each step moves very little. The draws are highly autocorrelated and the effective sample size is low. A very low acceptance rate signals the opposite problem (steps too large).
crumbs: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.7 Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and NUTS
Random-walk proposals are local and blind to the shape of the posterior. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) uses the gradient of the log posterior to make long, well-aimed proposals:

Picture the negative log posterior as a landscape and a frictionless marble on it. Give the marble a random push (momentum) and follow its path for a while with the leapfrog integrator. Where it stops is the proposal. It speeds up downhill and slows uphill, so it follows the shape of the posterior.
A Metropolis-style accept/reject step corrects for errors in the path. Proposals far away can still be accepted with high probability; Stan targets an acceptance rate of 0.8.
NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler) chooses the path length automatically: it stops when the trajectory starts to turn back on itself. It is Stan’s default.
Warm-up in Stan both discards early draws and tunes the step size and metric. Warm-up draws are never used for inference.

What can go wrong, and what brms tells you:








Warning
Meaning
Typical fix




Divergent transitions
The leapfrog path broke down in a region of sharp curvature (often a funnel in a hierarchical model). Draws may be biased.
Increase adapt_delta (e.g. 0.95, 0.99) for smaller steps; better, reparameterise or use more informative priors


Maximum treedepth exceeded
Paths hit the length limit, often because the posterior is very flat or elongated in some direction
Look for poorly identified parameters (Section 3.13); max_treedepth only helps with efficiency


High R-hat, low ESS
Chains disagree or are too autocorrelated
See Sections 3.8–3.10



HMC needs continuous parameters (the marble needs a smooth surface), so Stan cannot sample discrete parameters directly.

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.8 Convergence I: trace plots
Run several chains (brms default: 4) from different starting points. If they have all converged to the posterior they should be indistinguishable. A trace plot shows each parameter’s value against iteration, one colour per chain. Ask:

Are the chains stationary (no trend)?
Do they mix (overlap, cross each other constantly)?
Do they have the same mean and spread?









Figure 1: Four chains each, 300 iterations. Top left: converged and mixing well. Top right: converged but strongly autocorrelated (low ESS). Bottom left: drifting, not converged. Bottom right: stuck in two different modes.













Pattern
Likely cause
What to do




Autocorrelated but overlapping (2)
Slow exploration
Run longer; check ESS; reparameterise if extreme


Drift (3)
Warm-up too short; very slow chain
Run much longer; simplify or reparameterise


Chains in different places (4)
Multimodal posterior; poor identification
Rethink model and prior; running longer rarely rescues this



A single chain split in two can look fine while stuck in one mode: several chains from dispersed starting values are more likely to reveal a second mode. No diagnostic proves convergence: they can only detect non-convergence.

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
3.9 Convergence II: R-hat
The Gelman–Rubin statistic compares between-chain and within-chain variance, like an ANOVA. With \(m\) chains of length \(q\):
\[W = \frac{1}{m}\sum_j s_j^2, \qquad B = \frac{q}{m-1}\sum_j (\bar\theta_{\cdot j} - \bar\theta_{\cdot\cdot})^2, \qquad \widehat{\text{var}}^+ = \frac{q-1}{q}W + \frac{1}{q}B, \qquad \hat R = \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\text{var}}^+}{W}}.\]

If all chains sample the same distribution, \(B\) is small and \(\hat R \approx 1\).
Chains stuck apart, or still travelling from their starting values, inflate \(B\) and give \(\hat R > 1\).
Modern R-hat (the one brms reports) splits each chain in half first, so a single drifting chain is also detected, and uses rank-normalisation so heavy tails do not break it.

Rules of thumb. The course notes use \(\hat R < 1.1\). brms warns above 1.05. Current Stan advice (Vehtari et al., 2021) is \(\hat R < 1.01\) for final results. Check R-hat for every parameter; look at trace plots for the ones that fail.

  About 1.00, since each chain looks stable
  Well above 1, as the chain means differ
  Exactly 1.1, the conventional cut-off value
  Undefined, since the means cancel out
  B is large relative to W, so var⁺ is much larger than W and R-hat is far above 1. This is the multimodal pattern in panel 4: each chain looks fine on its own, but they disagree.

title: Module 3 — Model Fitting with Markov Chain Monte Carlo
section: 3.10 Convergence III: effective sample size and MCSE
text:
3.10 Convergence III: effective sample size and MCSE
With autocorrelation \(\rho_t\) at lag \(t\), \(m\) chains of \(q\) draws carry as much information as
\[n_\text{eff} = \frac{mq}{1 + 2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \rho_t}\]
independent draws. Strong autocorrelation means a small ESS. The MCSE of the posterior mean is about \(\text{posterior SD}/\sqrt{n_\text{eff}}\).
brms reports two ESS values:

Bulk_ESS: for the centre of the distribution (mean, median, SD).
Tail_ESS: for the 5% and 95% quantiles, and so for credible interval limits. Tails need more draws.

Rules of thumb (course notes). Bulk ESS ≥ 1,000 for posterior means and SDs: then \(1/\sqrt{1000} \approx 3\%\), so the MCSE is about 3% of the posterior SD. Stan’s warnings trigger below 100 per chain. For extreme quantiles or rare events you need more.
Thinning (keeping every \(k\)-th draw) lowers autocorrelation but throws information away. With NUTS the advice is to keep all post-warm-up draws; thinning only helps when memory is the bottleneck.

  Nothing, since R-hat shows convergence
  Run more iterations to raise the ESS
  Thin the chains to reduce autocorrelation
  Increase adapt_delta to 0.99 and refit
  R-hat ≈ 1 says the chains agree; ESS says how precise the Monte Carlo estimates are. With ESS = 150 the MCSE is about 8% of the posterior SD. Running longer raises the ESS. Thinning would lower it further.

The syllabus asks you to “prepare tables and figures that summarise the estimand(s) … by manipulating the sample from the joint posterior”. Three brms functions, each returning a matrix of draws × observations:








Function
Gives draws of…
Example (logistic model)

the linear predictor \(\eta_i = \alpha + \beta x_i\)
log-odds

Any estimand, computed draw by draw. Take as_draws_df(fit), compute your quantity for each row, then summarise:

draws$std_effect <- draws$b_treated / draws$sigma          # standardised effect

text:
3.13 Poorly identified models
If the data cannot distinguish some parameter combinations, the posterior is a long flat ridge: only a combination is identified. Example: body weight entered twice, once in kg and once in pounds. Only \(\beta_\text{kg} + 2.2046\,\beta_\text{lb}\) is identified. With vague priors the chains wander along the ridge: huge R-hat, tiny ESS, maximum-treedepth warnings (Task 3.3 below).

A more informative prior makes the posterior proper and the chains converge, but then the split between the two coefficients comes entirely from the prior.
The honest fix is usually a simpler model. Poor convergence is often the first sign of a model problem: nearly collinear predictors, many interactions with sparse cells, too many latent variables.

The notes’ advice: when chains misbehave, fit a simpler model to see whether identifiability is the cause.

Which step size gives a chain you would trust? Describe what goes wrong in the other two.

In RStudio: brms tasks






ImportantHow the RStudio tasks work



Each task simulates its own data, so you can run it straight away. Try it yourself first, then open the solution. The solutions were run with brms 2.23; your numbers will differ slightly (Monte Carlo error). Download all Module 3 tasks as one script: module3-tasks.R.



Task 3.1 · Your first brms model: an intercept and a standard deviation
Twelve runners’ resting heart rates (simulated): set.seed(510); runners <- data.frame(heart_rate = round(rnorm(12, mean = 58, sd = 7))).
Fit heart_rate ~ 1 with a Gaussian likelihood, prior normal(70, 15) for the intercept and exponential(0.1) for sigma.

Check the diagnostics before anything else. Are R-hat and ESS acceptable?
Compare the posterior mean with the sample mean. Which way did the prior pull, and why so little?
Compute \(P(\mu < 60 \mid y)\) and a 90% credible interval from the draws.







TipSolution





fit_hr <- brm(heart_rate ~ 1, family = gaussian(),
              prior = c(prior(normal(70, 15), class = "Intercept"),
                        prior(exponential(0.1), class = "sigma")),
              data = runners, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 510, refresh = 0)
summary(fit_hr)
plot(fit_hr)
draws_hr <- as_draws_df(fit_hr)
mean(draws_hr$b_Intercept < 60)
quantile(draws_hr$b_Intercept, c(0.05, 0.95))
What we got: Intercept 58.56 (SD 2.55), sigma 8.92, Rhat 1.00, Bulk_ESS ≈ 2,400 for both. Diagnostics fine. The sample mean is 58.25, so the prior (centred on 70) pulled the estimate up by only 0.3: the prior SD of 15 is wide compared with the data’s standard error (about 9/√12 ≈ 2.6). \(P(\mu < 60) \approx 0.73\); 90% interval 54.4 to 62.8.





Task 3.2 · A treatment effect, and quantities computed from draws
Simulated trial, 30 patients per arm:
set.seed(511)
trial <- data.frame(treated = rep(c(0, 1), each = 30))
trial$sbp_change <- rnorm(60, mean = -2 - 6 * trial$treated, sd = 8)
Fit sbp_change ~ treated with priors normal(0, 20) (Intercept), normal(0, 10) (b) and exponential(0.1) (sigma).

Compute the posterior of the standardised effect \(\beta/\sigma\) and a 95% interval.
What is the probability that the drug lowers SBP by more than 5 mmHg?
Use posterior_linpred() and posterior_predict() with newdata = data.frame(treated = c(0, 1)). Compare their SDs and explain the difference.
Rebuild both for the treated group by hand from as_draws_df() and check that you get the same.







TipSolution





fit_trial <- brm(sbp_change ~ treated, family = gaussian(),
                 prior = c(prior(normal(0, 20), class = "Intercept"),
                           prior(normal(0, 10), class = "b"),
                           prior(exponential(0.1), class = "sigma")),
                 data = trial, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 511, refresh = 0)
draws_trial <- as_draws_df(fit_trial)
draws_trial$std_effect <- draws_trial$b_treated / draws_trial$sigma
quantile(draws_trial$std_effect, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
mean(draws_trial$b_treated < -5)

new_patients <- data.frame(treated = c(0, 1))
apply(posterior_linpred(fit_trial, newdata = new_patients), 2, sd)
apply(posterior_predict(fit_trial, newdata = new_patients), 2, sd)

mu_treated <- draws_trial$b_Intercept + draws_trial$b_treated
y_treated  <- rnorm(nrow(draws_trial), mu_treated, draws_trial$sigma)
c(sd(mu_treated), sd(y_treated))
What we got: treated −5.89 (95% CrI −9.39 to −2.26), sigma 7.24. Standardised effect: median −0.82, 95% interval −1.35 to −0.30. \(P(\beta < -5) \approx 0.69\).
SD of the mean (linpred) ≈ 1.3 in each arm; SD of a new patient (predict) ≈ 7.4. The mean is estimated from 30 patients, but one new patient also varies with SD σ ≈ 7.2 around that mean: \(\sqrt{1.3^2 + 7.2^2} \approx 7.4\). The by-hand versions give the same (1.29 and 7.45).





Task 3.3 · When the chains do not converge
The same body weight in two units:
set.seed(512)
bodyweight <- data.frame(weight_kg = rnorm(50, mean = 75, sd = 12))
bodyweight$weight_lb <- bodyweight$weight_kg * 2.2046
bodyweight$sbp <- rnorm(50, mean = 100 + 0.4 * bodyweight$weight_kg, sd = 8)

Fit sbp ~ weight_kg + weight_lb with a vague normal(0, 1000) prior on the slopes (Intercept normal(120, 30), sigma exponential(0.1), iter = 1000). Read the warnings, R-hat and ESS. Look at the trace plots of the two slopes.
Compute b_weight_kg + 2.2046 * b_weight_lb draw by draw. Is that well estimated?
Refit with a normal(0, 1) prior on the slopes. What changes, and what does the prior now decide?







TipSolution





fit_both_vague <- brm(sbp ~ weight_kg + weight_lb, family = gaussian(),
                      prior = c(prior(normal(120, 30), class = "Intercept"),
                                prior(normal(0, 1000), class = "b"),
                                prior(exponential(0.1), class = "sigma")),
                      data = bodyweight, chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 512, refresh = 0)
summary(fit_both_vague)
plot(fit_both_vague, variable = c("b_weight_kg", "b_weight_lb"))
draws_vague <- as_draws_df(fit_both_vague)
effect_per_kg <- draws_vague$b_weight_kg + 2.2046 * draws_vague$b_weight_lb
summarise_draws(data.frame(effect_per_kg), "mean", "sd", "rhat", "ess_bulk")
What we got with the vague prior: weight_kg 333 ± 789 and weight_lb −151 ± 358, Rhat 2.68, Bulk_ESS 5, and warnings that 1,843 of 2,000 transitions exceeded the maximum treedepth. The chains wander along the ridge. Yet the identified combination is fine: effect per kg 0.22 (SD 0.11), Rhat 1.00, ESS ≈ 2,000.
With normal(0, 1): the model converges (Rhat ≤ 1.01, ESS ≈ 750), weight_kg 0.02 ± 0.93 and weight_lb 0.09 ± 0.42. The combination is still 0.02 + 2.2046 × 0.09 ≈ 0.22, but how it is split between the two coefficients is decided entirely by the prior. The real fix is to drop one of the two variables.
(The simulation used 0.4 mmHg per kg; with 50 people the estimate 0.22 ± 0.11 is within about two posterior SDs of that.)

Why-questions






NoteWhy does Metropolis only need the unnormalised posterior?





It only uses the ratio \(p(\theta^* \mid y)/p(\theta \mid y)\). The normalising constant appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels. Computing that constant is exactly the integral we could not do.









NoteWhy run several chains rather than one long chain?





Chains started in different places that end up agreeing are evidence of convergence. A single chain stuck in one mode can look perfectly stationary. R-hat needs several chains, and they run in parallel on several cores.









NoteWhy is R-hat ≈ 1 not enough?





R-hat checks that chains agree, not that you have enough information. Also check the ESS (precision of the estimates), divergent transitions (possible bias) and, separately, whether the model fits the data (Module 4).

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
Every Bayesian analysis in this course is the same machine: prior × likelihood → posterior, and then everything you want to know (a best guess, an interval, a probability, a prediction, a decision) is read off the posterior. Module 1 shows that machine in the simplest possible setting, where the parameter can only take a list of values and Bayes’ rule is just multiplication followed by division by a sum. No integrals and no MCMC yet.
The module opens with the philosophical difference that drives everything else: what is a probability? The classical (frequentist) definition only allows probabilities for repeatable events, so a fixed but unknown parameter cannot have one. The Bayesian definition treats probability as a measure of uncertainty, so a parameter, a unique event or a future observation can all have a probability distribution.
That difference has practical consequences. It is why a credible interval can say “the parameter is in here with 95% probability” and a confidence interval cannot, and why Bayesian models can predict new data directly. The examples on this page are made up for this app: a thyroid screening test, a treatment decision and a count of fish in a pond.
The page has two parts. Part A (concepts, no code needed) covers the ideas; mark each section as you go. Part B runs small R examples in your browser.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
1.1 Two meanings of probability









Frequentist (classical)
Bayesian




Probability is…
the long-run relative frequency of an event in infinitely many repetitions under identical conditions
a number between 0 and 1 that measures uncertainty (partial knowledge) about anything unknown


Can have a probability
repeatable events: the next coin toss, a random sample
also unique events and fixed unknown quantities: “this patient has the disease”, “the true mean is above 5”


Parameters are…
fixed constants; randomness is only in the data
unknown, so described by a distribution


Typical output
estimator, standard error, p-value, confidence interval
posterior distribution, credible interval, posterior predictive distribution



Two problems with the frequency definition: “identical conditions” is vague (the same coin, the same person tossing it, the same air pressure?) and, more seriously, many events cannot be repeated even in principle. Whether it rained in Gothenburg on 1 September 2026, or whether this particular patient responds to treatment, has no long-run frequency. Yet weather services publish a probability of rain every day, and clinicians talk about a patient’s probability of disease. The Bayesian view makes that everyday usage formal.






WarningCommon confusion: “Bayesian means subjective, so it is less scientific”



Every analysis contains choices: which data to collect, which model to fit, which variables to adjust for, which results to report. The prior is one more choice, and it is written down explicitly where others can inspect and vary it. The course notes deliberately put the prior last in the list of error sources: data errors, software errors and model misspecification are usually more dangerous and harder to detect.



  The test will be positive in about 5% of healthy people
  There is a 0.8 probability that this drug lowers blood pressure
  If we resample, 95% of such intervals will cover the true mean
  The p-value is the probability of data this extreme under H0
  “This drug lowers blood pressure” is a statement about a fixed unknown quantity (the true effect). Under the frequentist definition it is simply true or false and has no probability. The other three are statements about repeatable data-generating events.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
1.2 Why use probability for beliefs?
The notes give three justifications. None is a proof; each makes the Bayesian approach reasonable.

Analogy. We already describe physical randomness with probability. Using the same language for uncertainty due to incomplete knowledge is natural.
Decision theory. Decisions under uncertainty should minimise expected loss. If you want to act rationally on uncertain information, you need numbers that behave like probabilities.
Coherence of bets. If the prices you would pay for bets on events do not obey the rules of probability, a bookmaker can arrange bets so that you lose money whatever happens (a “Dutch book”).


Worked example: when to treat. Suppose treating a healthy patient costs 1 unit (side effects, cost), and not treating a sick patient costs 9 units. Let \(p\) be the probability that the patient is sick.



Decision
Expected loss




Treat
\((1-p) \times 1\)


Do not treat
\(p \times 9\)



Treat when \((1-p) < 9p\), that is when \(p > 1/10\). In general, treat when
\[p > \frac{\text{cost of a false positive}}{\text{cost of a false positive} + \text{cost of a false negative}}.\]
This threshold is the same for every patient. What differs is \(p\), and \(p\) is specific to this patient with these symptoms. A single long-run frequency cannot provide it; a probability for the individual case can.

A decision that minimises expected loss can still turn out badly for a particular patient. Decision theory only promises the best average over repeated decisions made with the information available at the time.

  0.25
  0.20
  0.80
  0.50
  Threshold = 1 / (1 + 4) = 0.20. Treat if P(sick) > 0.20.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
section: 1.3 Bayes’ rule and the base-rate fallacy
text:
1.3 Bayes’ rule and the base-rate fallacy
\[p(B \mid A) = \frac{p(A \mid B)\, p(B)}{p(A)} = \frac{p(A \mid B)\, p(B)}{\sum_b p(A \mid B = b)\, p(B = b)}\]
Bayes’ rule follows directly from the definition of conditional probability. Nobody disputes it. The debate between schools of statistics is about which quantities may have probability distributions, not about the rule itself.

Worked example: screening for hypothyroidism. In a screening population 2% have the condition. The test has sensitivity 0.95 (positive when sick) and specificity 0.90 (negative when healthy). A person tests positive. What is the probability that they have the condition?
Think in natural frequencies, 10,000 people:




Test positive
Test negative
Total




Condition
190
10
200


No condition
980
8,820
9,800


Total
1,170
8,830
10,000



\[P(\text{condition} \mid +) = \frac{0.95 \times 0.02}{0.95 \times 0.02 + 0.10 \times 0.98} = \frac{190}{1170} \approx 0.16\]
Only 16%, despite a test that is right 95% and 90% of the time. There are more false positives (980) than true positives (190) because healthy people vastly outnumber sick people. Ignoring the prevalence (the prior) is the base-rate fallacy. Using Bayes’ rule is uncontroversial here: the fallacy comes from not using it.

Vocabulary that maps directly onto Bayesian terms:







Diagnostic testing
Bayesian inference




Prevalence, pre-test probability
Prior \(p(\theta)\)


Sensitivity and specificity
Likelihood \(p(y \mid \theta)\)


Positive predictive value, post-test probability
Posterior \(p(\theta \mid y)\)









WarningCommon confusion: the p-value is not P(H0 | data)



A p-value is (roughly) \(P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)\). Reading it as \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data})\) swaps the condition, the same mistake as reading sensitivity as the positive predictive value. Getting from one to the other requires Bayes’ rule, and therefore a prior probability for \(H_0\).



  It stays at 0.16, because the test is unchanged
  It rises to about 0.70, as the prior is higher
  It rises to 0.95, which is the test’s sensitivity
  It falls, because more people are now tested
  PPV = 0.95 × 0.20 / (0.95 × 0.20 + 0.10 × 0.80) = 0.19 / 0.27 ≈ 0.70. The likelihood (test accuracy) is unchanged; the prior (prevalence) changed, so the posterior changed.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
section: 1.4 A whole posterior from a discrete prior
text:
1.4 A whole posterior from a discrete prior
Screening had one number as the answer. Usually the unknown can take many values and we want its whole posterior distribution. With a discrete parameter this still only needs multiplication and one sum.

Worked example: how many fish are in the pond? You catch, mark and release 30 fish. A week later you catch 25 fish and 5 of them carry a mark. Let \(N\) be the number of fish in the pond.
Likelihood. If the pond has \(N\) fish and fish mix freely, the number of marked fish in a catch of 25 follows a hypergeometric distribution:
\[p(y = 5 \mid N) = \frac{\binom{30}{5}\binom{N-30}{20}}{\binom{N}{25}}\]
It is zero for \(N < 50\): you have already seen \(30 + 20 = 50\) different fish. The maximum likelihood estimate is about \(30 \times 25 / 5 = 150\) (the classical Lincoln–Petersen estimate).
Prior. A local angler says “a few hundred, probably not more than a thousand”. A log-normal distribution with median 300 and log-scale SD 0.6 puts about 95% of its mass between roughly 90 and 1000. Restrict it to \(N = 50, \dots, 3000\) and rescale so it sums to one.
Bayes’ rule on a grid. For every candidate \(N\): multiply prior × likelihood, then divide by the sum over all \(N\).









Figure 1: Prior (dashed), likelihood rescaled to sum to one (dotted) and posterior (solid) for the number of fish.





The posterior sits between the prior (median 300) and the likelihood (peak near 150): posterior mode 165, median 195, mean 213, and a 90% credible interval from 115 to 372. The prior pulls the estimate up because five recaptures out of 25 is little data. The likelihood’s long right tail (large ponds are hard to rule out with few recaptures) is tamed by the prior’s belief that ponds of 2,000 fish are unusual.
Two conditions for this to work, from the notes’ abbreviated workflow:

the likelihood must be defined for every value the prior allows (it may be zero for some), and
at least some values with non-zero prior must give the observed data non-zero probability. If the prior only allowed \(N < 50\), no posterior would exist.


  Nothing, because the data decide the posterior
  It moves to larger N, since the data are weak
  It moves to smaller N, towards the likelihood peak
  It becomes identical to the new, wider prior
  With little data the prior has a large influence. A prior centred on 1,000 pulls the posterior upwards. More recaptures (more data) would make the likelihood narrower and reduce the prior’s influence.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
1.5 Summarising a posterior
The posterior is the answer. Summaries are chosen for the reader and the decision at hand.








Summary
Definition
Best under loss…




Posterior mean
\(E[\theta \mid y]\)
squared error


Posterior median
50th percentile
absolute error


Posterior mode (MAP)
\(\arg\max_\theta p(\theta \mid y)\)
“all or nothing” (0–1 loss)


Posterior SD
SD of the posterior
describes uncertainty about \(\theta\)


Equal-tailed 95% credible interval
2.5th to 97.5th percentile
easy, works with transformations


95% highest posterior density (HPD) interval
shortest region containing 95%
can be several pieces if the posterior has several modes



A 95% credible interval means what people usually want a confidence interval to mean: given the model, the prior and the data, \(\theta\) lies in the interval with probability 0.95.
Transformations. Because a monotone transformation keeps the order of values, interval endpoints transform directly: if \([-0.40, 0.10]\) is a 95% credible interval for a log relative risk, then \([e^{-0.40}, e^{0.10}] = [0.67, 1.11]\) is a 95% credible interval for the relative risk. Means do not: \(E[e^{\theta}] \neq e^{E[\theta]}\). The median transforms directly because it is a percentile.
With a sample of draws (from Module 3 on, MCMC gives you draws from the posterior), every summary becomes an average or a percentile over draws. A derived quantity, such as a ratio of two parameters, is computed draw by draw, which keeps the correlation between parameters intact.






WarningCommon confusion: three different spreads



Data SD (\(\sigma\)): how much individual observations vary. Posterior SD of a mean: how uncertain you are about the mean; it shrinks as \(n\) grows, like a standard error. Posterior predictive SD: how uncertain you are about one new observation; it never shrinks below \(\sigma\). A larger \(\sigma\) usually means larger posterior and predictive SDs too, but they answer different questions.



  The posterior mean OR is exactly exp(0.40)
  The 95% interval for OR is [exp(0.10), exp(0.70)]
  The posterior SD of OR is exp of the SD of log(OR)
  Transforming an interval needs the delta method
  Percentiles (and so equal-tailed interval endpoints and the median) survive monotone transformations. Means and SDs do not: E[exp(θ)] > exp(E[θ]) for a spread-out posterior. With draws you would simply compute exp() for every draw and summarise the result.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
1.6 Posterior predictive distributions
Bayesian models are generative: given parameter values, you can simulate new data. Integrating over the posterior gives the posterior predictive distribution:
\[p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta\]
It is easiest to compute by Monte Carlo:

Posterior predictive by Monte Carlo

Repeat many times: (a) draw \(\theta^{(s)}\) from the posterior; (b) draw a new \(\tilde y^{(s)}\) from \(p(y \mid \theta^{(s)})\).
Summarise the \(\tilde y^{(s)}\): a mean, a probability such as \(P(\tilde y \geq 10)\), or an expected loss.


Fish example: next week you catch 40 fish. Each posterior draw of \(N\) gives one simulated number of marked fish. Because \(N\) is uncertain, the predictive distribution is wider than a hypergeometric distribution with \(N\) fixed at its posterior mean. Plugging in a single best guess underestimates uncertainty.
To check whether you ran enough Monte Carlo draws, rerun the simulation and look at how much the answer changes: that variation is the Monte Carlo error. More draws shrink it at the rate \(1/\sqrt{\text{number of draws}}\).
Conditionally generative models. A regression model predicts \(y\) given \(X\); it does not model the covariates themselves. That is fine when you choose \(X\) (a dose, a treatment). Not every method is generative: a permutation test gives a p-value but cannot say what the next observation will look like.

  Because Monte Carlo sampling adds noise
  It also includes the uncertainty about θ itself
  Because the prior is added to the likelihood twice
  It is not wider; the two are identical
  Predictive uncertainty = sampling variation of a new observation + uncertainty about the parameter. Fixing θ drops the second part.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
1.7 The Bayesian workflow, abbreviated
The notes give a four-step version here and expand it in Module 6:

Full probability model for everything: observed data, unknown parameters, future or missing data. Requires knowing the research question and how the data were collected.
Prior: express the available information about the unknowns as a joint prior distribution.
Condition on the data: compute the posterior (and posterior predictive) of the quantities of interest.
Evaluate: does the model fit the data? Are the conclusions reasonable? How sensitive are they to the model and the prior?

Step 4 usually sends you back to step 1 or 2: the workflow is a loop, not a line. Modules 3 and 4 give the tools for step 4.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
section: 1.8 Confidence intervals are not credible intervals
text:
1.8 Confidence intervals are not credible intervals
Both are abbreviated “CI” and with large samples they often agree numerically. They answer different questions.


95% confidence interval
A property of the procedure: if the experiment were repeated infinitely often, 95% of the intervals produced would contain the true value. Says nothing about this interval.


95% credible interval
A property of this posterior: given the model, prior and data, the parameter lies in the interval with probability 0.95.


Why a confidence interval cannot be read as a credible interval (the notes’ argument, with made-up numbers):

Coverage is about the procedure, not the interval. “Flip a coin: heads, report \((-\infty, \infty)\); tails, report the single point \(\{0\}\)” is a valid 50% confidence procedure for any non-zero parameter. It never uses the data. Its intervals are either useless or almost certainly wrong, yet the procedure has exact 50% coverage. So the width of a confidence interval does not by itself measure precision.
Several valid procedures give different intervals for the same data. With 4 successes out of 20:






Interval
Lower
Upper




Wald 95% CI
0.025
0.375


Wilson 95% CI
0.081
0.416


Exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% CI
0.057
0.437


95% credible interval, Beta(1, 1) prior
0.082
0.419





If every valid 95% confidence interval were a 95% probability statement about \(\theta\), the region between the Wilson and exact limits would have to contain both 0% and a positive share of the probability. That is a contradiction. So confidence intervals are not automatically probability statements; at most one procedure could coincide with some posterior, and not because it is a confidence procedure.

A credible interval has no such contradiction: one prior + one model + one dataset gives exactly one posterior. Two people with different priors get different posteriors, just as two people with different data or models would.

Do credible intervals have 95% coverage in repeated experiments? Not in general. Coverage depends on how the prior relates to the true value: a prior that puts zero probability on the true value gives zero coverage. Module 2, Section 2.8 shows this in a simulation.






WarningCommon confusion: “95% of the time, the true value lies in my confidence interval”



The true value is fixed and your interval is fixed: it either contains the value or not. The 95% refers to the long run of hypothetical repetitions. The sentence “there is a 95% probability that the effect lies between A and B” is a credible-interval statement and needs a prior.



  Correct, that is the definition of a confidence interval
  That is a credible-interval statement; it needs a prior
  Correct, as long as the sample size is above 30
  Only true for the exact interval, not for the Wald one
  The 95% of a confidence interval refers to the procedure over repeated samples. A probability statement about the parameter itself requires a posterior, and so a prior. With a flat prior and a large sample the numbers are often close, which is why the confusion is common.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
1.9 Hypothesis tests and Bayes factors
You can compute \(P(\theta > 0 \mid y)\) from a posterior. Two cautions from the notes:

It depends on the prior probability that \(\theta > 0\). If you then dichotomise at 0.05, two reasonable priors can give 0.049 and 0.051 and opposite decisions.
For a continuous parameter \(P(\theta = 0 \mid y) = 0\): a point null always has zero posterior probability.

The Bayes factor compares whole models instead:
\[\underbrace{\frac{p(m_1 \mid y)}{p(m_2 \mid y)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} = \underbrace{\frac{p(y \mid m_1)}{p(y \mid m_2)}}_{\text{Bayes factor}} \times \underbrace{\frac{p(m_1)}{p(m_2)}}_{\text{prior odds}}\]
BF > 1 favours \(m_1\). The Bayes factor does not depend on the prior odds of the models, but it does depend on the priors for the parameters inside each model: a vague prior for an effect in \(m_1\) spreads prior mass over huge effects and lowers \(p(y \mid m_1)\). You must specify what the alternative hypothesis looks like. The course notes do not use hypothesis testing after Module 1. Later modules compare models by predictive performance instead (Module 4).

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
section: When does the Bayesian answer differ most?
text:
When does the Bayesian answer differ most?

Small samples and strong prior information: the prior visibly moves the answer (the fish example).
Unique events and decisions: a probability for this patient, this trial, or an expected loss.
Parameters near a boundary (proportions near 0 or 1, variances near 0), where classical intervals can include impossible values.
With large samples and weak priors the likelihood dominates and Bayesian and classical results usually agree numerically, though their interpretations still differ.

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
Limitations

The answer depends on the prior and the model. That dependence is visible and can be checked (sensitivity analysis), but it cannot be removed.
Translating vague knowledge (“probably small”) into a specific distribution is hard, and “I have no idea” cannot be expressed exactly (see flat priors in Module 2).
A grid over all parameter values only works for one or two parameters. Beyond that, computation needs MCMC (Module 3).

title: Module 1 — Bayesian Concepts
text:
Why-questions






NoteWhy is Bayes’ rule uncontroversial but Bayesian statistics debated?





Bayes’ rule is a theorem of probability. The debate is about whether unknown fixed quantities (parameters, hypotheses, unique events) may have probability distributions, and so whether a prior may be used at all.









NoteWhy does the prior matter less as the sample grows?





The likelihood is a product over observations, so it becomes more and more concentrated while the prior stays the same. Eventually the likelihood dominates the product prior × likelihood. The exception: values with zero prior probability stay impossible whatever the data say.









NoteWhy should the posterior predictive not use a single best estimate?





A single estimate ignores the uncertainty about the parameter, so predictions are too narrow and rare events look rarer than they are. Tail events (extreme values, rare adverse outcomes) are where this matters most.

title: Glossary
text:
A–C

Adapt delta (adapt_delta)

Stan’s target acceptance rate during warm-up (default 0.8). Raising it (0.95, 0.99) gives smaller steps and fewer divergent transitions, at the cost of speed. M3 §3.7

AIC

Akaike information criterion: −2 × log-likelihood at the maximum + 2 × number of parameters. Ignores posterior uncertainty. M4 §4.7

Autocorrelation

Correlation between MCMC draws a given number of iterations apart. High autocorrelation lowers the effective sample size. M3 §3.10

Base-rate fallacy

Ignoring the prior probability (prevalence) when interpreting evidence, e.g. reading sensitivity as the positive predictive value. M1 §1.3

Bayes factor

Ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two models; turns prior odds into posterior odds. Depends on the priors inside each model. M1 §1.9

Bayes’ rule

\(p(\theta \mid y) = p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta) / p(y)\). M1 §1.3

Bayesian model averaging (pseudo-BMA)

Averaging predictive distributions with weights proportional to \(\exp(-\tfrac12 \text{WAIC})\) or the LOO equivalent. M4 §4.10

Beta–Binomial

The conjugate pair Beta prior + binomial likelihood (posterior Beta(a + y, b + n − y)), and the posterior predictive distribution of a new count. M2 §2.6 · §2.9

Bias–variance trade-off

MSE = bias² + variance. Shrinkage accepts some bias for a larger drop in variance. M5 §5.9

brms

R package that turns an lme4-style formula into a Stan program and fits it with NUTS. M3 §3.11

Burn-in / warm-up

Initial MCMC iterations that are discarded. In Stan, warm-up also tunes the sampler. M3 §3.4 · §3.7

Calibration

Frequentist properties (bias, coverage) of a Bayesian procedure, studied by simulation. M6 §6.6

Complete pooling

All groups assumed identical; one common parameter. M5 §5.2

Confidence interval

An interval from a procedure that covers the true value in a stated share of hypothetical repetitions. Not a probability statement about the parameter. M1 §1.8

Conjugate prior

A prior whose posterior belongs to the same family, so updating is arithmetic on its parameters. M2 §2.6

Coverage

The share of intervals that contain the true value over repeated experiments. M2 §2.8

Credible interval

An interval containing the parameter with a stated posterior probability, given model, prior and data. Equal-tailed or HPD. M1 §1.5

Crossed random effects

Grouping factors that are not nested, e.g. region and survey round. M5 §5.7

title: Glossary
text:
D–K

DIC

Deviance information criterion: posterior mean deviance plus a penalty from the posterior variance of the deviance. M4 §4.7

Divergent transition

An HMC trajectory that broke down in a region of high curvature; a sign the draws may be biased. M3 §3.7

Effective sample size (ESS; bulk and tail)

The number of independent draws with the same information as the autocorrelated MCMC draws. Bulk for means and SDs, tail for interval limits. M3 §3.10

elpd

Expected log pointwise predictive density for new data; the target that WAIC and LOO estimate. Higher is better. M4 §4.6

Empirical Bayes

Estimate the hyperparameters from the data, then plug them in as known. Ignores their uncertainty. M5 §5.3

Equivalent sample size

How many observations a prior is “worth”; a + b − 2 for Beta(a, b) in the notes’ convention. M2 §2.7

Estimand

The quantity that answers the research question, often computed from parameters draw by draw. M4 §4.11 · Project step 1

Gamma–Poisson

Conjugate pair for rates: Gamma(α, β) prior, Poisson counts with exposure E, posterior Gamma(α + y, β + E). M2 §2.10

Generative model

A model that can simulate new data from parameters; required for posterior predictive distributions. M1 §1.6

Gibbs sampler

MCMC that samples each parameter from its full conditional distribution in turn. M3 §3.5

GLMM

Generalised linear mixed model: a GLM with group-level (random) effects. M5 §5.7

Grid approximation

Evaluating prior × likelihood on a grid and normalising by the sum. Works for one or two parameters. M1 §1.4 · M2 §2.1

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)

MCMC that uses the gradient of the log posterior to make long, well-aimed proposals. M3 §3.7

HPD interval

Highest posterior density interval: the shortest region containing the stated probability. M1 §1.5

Hyperprior / hyperparameter

The prior on the parameters of the group-level distribution (e.g. μ and τ). M5 §5.3

Improper prior

A “prior” that does not integrate to 1, e.g. flat on the real line. May or may not give a proper posterior. M2 §2.4

Jeffreys’ prior

\(p(\theta) \propto \sqrt{I(\theta)}\); invariant under reparameterisation. M6 §6.7

Kullback–Leibler divergence

\(\int g \log(g/f)\): a non-negative, asymmetric measure of how far a predictive distribution f is from the true g. M4 §4.6

title: Glossary
text:
L–P

Likelihood

\(p(y \mid \theta)\) as a function of θ for fixed data. M1

linpred / epred / predict

brms functions giving draws of the linear predictor, the expected outcome, and a new observation. M3 §3.12

LKJ prior

Prior for correlation matrices of varying effects; lkj(2) mildly favours correlations near 0. M5 §5.8

LOO-CV / PSIS-LOO

Leave-one-out cross-validation, approximated from one fit by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling. M4 §4.8

loo_compare

Ranks models by elpd; reports each model’s difference from the best and the SE of the difference. M4 §4.9

MAP

Maximum a posteriori: the posterior mode. M1 §1.5

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)

Algorithms that generate a dependent sequence of draws whose distribution converges to the posterior. M3 §3.4

Median odds ratio (MOR)

\(\exp(0.954\,\tau)\) for a logistic GLMM: the median odds ratio between two random groups. Project step 1

Metropolis(–Hastings)

MCMC that proposes a move and accepts it with probability min(1, posterior ratio), corrected for asymmetric proposals in MH. M3 §3.6

Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)

The simulation error of an MCMC or Monte Carlo estimate; about posterior SD / √ESS for a mean. M3 §3.2 · §3.10

No pooling

Each group estimated from its own data only. M5 §5.2

NUTS

No-U-Turn Sampler: HMC that chooses its path length automatically; Stan’s default. M3 §3.7

Pareto k̂

Diagnostic per observation in PSIS-LOO; values above 0.7 make the approximation unreliable. M4 §4.8

Partial pooling

Group estimates shrunk towards the population mean by an amount learned from the data; the hierarchical model. M5 §5.2

Posterior predictive check (PPC)

Comparing replicated data from the fitted model with the observed data. M4 §4.2

Posterior predictive distribution

The distribution of new data after integrating over the posterior. M1 §1.6

Posterior predictive p-value

\(P(T(y^\text{rep}) \geq T(y) \mid y)\); near 0 or 1 signals misfit for statistic T. M4 §4.3

Precision

1 / variance. In the normal–normal model, precisions add. M2 §2.2

Prior predictive check

Simulating data from the prior alone to see what the prior implies; sample_prior = "only" in brms. M6 §6.2

title: Glossary
text:
R–Z

R-hat (Gelman–Rubin)

Ratio of total to within-chain variability; ≈ 1 when chains agree. The notes use < 1.1, current Stan advice < 1.01. M3 §3.9

Reference prior

A prior chosen to maximise the data’s influence (expected KL divergence from prior to posterior). M6 §6.7

Rejection sampling

Draw from a proposal and accept with probability f/(c·g); exact but inefficient in many dimensions. M3 §3.3

Sensitivity analysis (prior)

Refitting with alternative priors to see whether conclusions change. M6 §6.5

Sequential updating

Using the posterior from one dataset as the prior for the next; gives the same result as one combined analysis. M2 §2.5

Shrinkage

Pulling an estimate towards a prior or population mean, more for noisier estimates. M2 §2.3 · M5 §5.4

Simulation-based calibration (SBC)

Checking that posterior quantiles of true values drawn from the prior are uniform. M6 §6.6

Stacking

Weighting models’ predictive distributions to maximise LOO predictive performance of the mixture. M4 §4.10

Student-t likelihood

Heavy-tailed alternative to the normal, robust to outliers; family = student(). M4 §4.5

Temporal coherence

Specifying the prior before seeing the data and not revising it; broken whenever the data guide model changes. M6 §6.3

Test statistic T(y)

A summary of the data used in a posterior predictive check. M4 §4.3

Thinning

Keeping every k-th draw. Lowers autocorrelation but discards information; rarely useful with NUTS. M3 §3.10

Trace plot

Parameter value against iteration, one line per chain. M3 §3.8

Varying slopes

Group-specific slopes (and usually intercepts) with a covariance matrix: (1 + x | group). M5 §5.8

WAIC

Widely applicable information criterion: −2 × (lppd − p_WAIC), fully pointwise and Bayesian. M4 §4.7

Weakly informative prior

A prior that rules out absurd values but otherwise lets the data speak. M6 §6.4

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
text:
In Module 1 the parameter could only take a list of values, so Bayes’ rule needed a sum. Most parameters are continuous (a mean, a proportion, a rate), and then the denominator of Bayes’ rule is an integral. Integrals are hard in general. This module covers the special cases where they are easy.
A prior is conjugate to a likelihood when the posterior belongs to the same family as the prior. Then updating is just arithmetic on the prior’s parameters: a Beta prior plus binomial data gives a Beta posterior, a Gamma prior plus Poisson counts gives a Gamma posterior, and a normal prior plus normal data with known variance gives a normal posterior.
Conjugate models show the logic of Bayesian inference with nothing hidden. The posterior mean is a compromise between the prior mean and the data, weighted by how informative each is. Precision adds up. The prior behaves like extra data with an equivalent sample size. The data are “shrunk” towards the prior, and this shrinkage returns in Module 5 as partial pooling.
Conjugacy runs out quickly. The list of conjugate pairs is short, and realistic models (Student-t errors, detection limits, several unknown parameters) leave it. That is the motivation for MCMC in Module 3.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
section: 2.1 From sums to integrals, and back to sums
text:
2.1 From sums to integrals, and back to sums
For a continuous parameter,
\[p(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta}.\]
The denominator is only a normalising constant: it makes the posterior integrate to 1. Two ways around it:

Calculus. For conjugate pairs the integral has a known answer: recognise the kernel of the posterior.
Approximate the integral by a sum (a Riemann sum). Evaluate prior × likelihood on a fine grid of \(\theta\) values, then divide by the sum times the grid width. This is exactly the Module 1 recipe, and it works well for one or two parameters.

A histogram of a large sample is the same idea in reverse: with enough draws and narrow bins it traces out the density. That is why a sample of posterior draws (Module 3) can stand in for the posterior itself.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
section: 2.2 Normal data with known variance: precision adds up
text:
2.2 Normal data with known variance: precision adds up
Data \(y_1, \dots, y_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known, prior \(\mu \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)\). The posterior is normal with
\[\frac{1}{\sigma_n^2} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sigma_0^2}}_{\text{prior precision}} + \underbrace{\frac{n}{\sigma^2}}_{\text{data precision}}, \qquad \mu_n = \frac{\frac{1}{\sigma_0^2}\mu_0 + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\bar y}{\frac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}}.\]

Precision adds: the posterior is always more precise than both the prior and the data alone, even if the data conflict with the prior.
The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
Only \(\bar y\) enters: it is a sufficient statistic here.


Worked example: a patient’s long-term HbA1c. Two measurements average \(\bar y = 50\) mmol/mol. Measurement variation (analytical + biological) is \(\sigma = 4\). In the patient’s age group, long-term HbA1c has mean 40 and SD 8; use that as the prior, \(N(40, 8^2)\).
