title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
section: 2.3 Shrinkage: three ways to write the same posterior mean
text:
2.3 Shrinkage: three ways to write the same posterior mean
\[\mu_n = \underbrace{w\,\mu_0 + (1-w)\,\bar y}_{\text{weighted average}} = \underbrace{\mu_0 + (\bar y - \mu_0)\frac{\sigma_0^2}{\sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2/n}}_{\text{prior adjusted towards the data}} = \underbrace{\bar y - (\bar y - \mu_0)\frac{\sigma^2/n}{\sigma^2/n + \sigma_0^2}}_{\text{data shrunk towards the prior}}\]
with \(w = \dfrac{1/\sigma_0^2}{1/\sigma_0^2 + n/\sigma^2}\).
The last form is shrinkage: the estimate is pulled from \(\bar y\) towards \(\mu_0\), and the fraction pulled is (sampling variance of \(\bar y\)) / (sampling variance + prior variance). Noisy data, or a confident prior, means more shrinkage.
Limits: \(\mu_n = \mu_0\) if \(\sigma_0^2 = 0\) (a prior certain of \(\mu_0\)); \(\mu_n = \bar y\) if \(\sigma^2 = 0\) or \(\sigma_0^2 \to \infty\).
Intuition from the HbA1c example: a patient measured higher than typical for their age. Part of that may be chance (two readings happened to be high), so the best estimate of their long-term value is slightly lower than their measured mean. With more readings, the chance explanation becomes less plausible and the shrinkage disappears. Module 5 applies exactly this to groups: small hospitals’ rates are shrunk towards the average hospital.

section: 2.4 Flat priors, improper priors and the classical interval
text:
2.4 Flat priors, improper priors and the classical interval
Let \(\sigma_0^2 \to \infty\): the prior becomes flat over the whole real line. The posterior becomes \(N(\bar y, \sigma^2/n)\), and the 95% credible interval is \(\bar y \pm 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\): numerically identical to the classical confidence interval, though still interpreted as a probability statement about \(\mu\).

A flat prior on the real line is improper: it does not integrate to 1. Here the posterior is still proper, but that is not guaranteed in general. An improper posterior cannot be used.
“Non-informative” is misleading. A flat prior says that \(\mu\) between 1 and 2 million is exactly as plausible as \(\mu\) between 1 and 2. That is rarely anybody’s actual belief.
Flat on one scale is not flat on another: flat on \(\sigma\) is not flat on \(\sigma^2\) or \(\log \sigma\) (Module 6).

2.5 Sequential updating
Today’s posterior is tomorrow’s prior. Updating with dataset 1 and then dataset 2 gives exactly the same posterior as updating once with both:
\[p(\theta \mid y_1, y_2) \propto p(y_2 \mid \theta)\,\underbrace{p(y_1 \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)}_{\propto\, p(\theta \mid y_1)}\]
(assuming \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are independent given \(\theta\)).

text:
2.6 Conjugacy and the Beta–Binomial model
\(y\) successes in \(n\) trials, \(y \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\), prior \(\theta \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)\):
\[p(\theta \mid y) \propto \underbrace{\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{n-y}}_{\text{likelihood}}\,\underbrace{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}_{\text{prior}} = \theta^{a+y-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-y-1} \;\Rightarrow\; \theta \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(a + y,\; b + n - y).\]
Add successes to \(a\), failures to \(b\). The mean of \(\text{Beta}(a, b)\) is \(a/(a+b)\), and
\[E[\theta \mid y] = \frac{a + y}{a + b + n} = w \cdot \frac{a}{a+b} + (1-w)\cdot\frac{y}{n}, \qquad w = \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}.\]
The same compromise as before: prior mean and sample proportion, weighted by their “sample sizes”.
Choosing \(a\) and \(b\) from a mean and an SD (method of moments). If the prior mean is \(m\) and prior SD is \(s\):
\[a + b = \frac{m(1-m)}{s^2} - 1, \qquad a = m\,(a+b), \qquad b = (1-m)(a+b).\]

Worked example: medication adherence. Similar adherence programmes achieved between about 40% and 80%, centred on 60%. Take \(m = 0.6\) and \(s = 0.1\) (so about 95% of the prior mass between 0.4 and 0.8): \(a + b = 0.24 / 0.01 - 1 = 23\), giving Beta(13.8, 9.2).

section: 2.7 The prior as data: equivalent sample size
text:
2.7 The prior as data: equivalent sample size
Compare the kernels: \(\text{Beta}(a, b) \propto \theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\) looks like a binomial likelihood with \(a - 1\) successes in \(a + b - 2\) trials. So a Beta prior behaves like \(a + b - 2\) earlier observations (the notes’ convention, counting from the uniform Beta(1, 1); some books use \(a + b\) instead).

Beta(1, 1), the uniform distribution: 0 prior observations. The posterior equals the normalised likelihood.
Beta(13.8, 9.2) from the adherence example: about 21 prior patients, similar to the 30 new ones, which is why the posterior landed roughly halfway.
Beta(0.5, 0.5) would be “−1 observations”: the analogy breaks, but the prior is still valid.

For the normal model the equivalent sample size is \(\sigma^2 / \sigma_0^2\): the prior is worth as much as that many observations. In the HbA1c example, \(16/64 = 0.25\) of a reading.
Why it matters. Before you use a prior, ask: “how many observations is this prior worth?” If a supposedly weak prior is worth 500 patients and your study has 100, it is not weak.

2.9 Posterior predictive: Beta–Binomial vs the naive plug-in
How many of the next \(\tilde n = 50\) patients will adhere?
\[p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int \text{Binomial}(\tilde y \mid \tilde n, \theta)\; \text{Beta}(\theta \mid a', b')\; d\theta = \text{Beta-Binomial}(\tilde y \mid \tilde n, a', b')\]








Figure 2: Predicted number of adherent patients out of 50. Left: correct posterior predictive (Beta-Binomial). Right: naive plug-in of the posterior mean into a binomial.





Both have mean \(50 \times 0.43 = 21.5\). The SD is 4.8 for the Beta–Binomial and 3.5 for the plug-in. The chance of at least 25 adherent patients is 0.27 vs 0.20: ignoring parameter uncertainty makes you overconfident, in the tails especially.
The mean of the predictive is just \(\tilde n \times E[\theta \mid y]\), which is why the posterior mean of \(\theta\) is also the predictive probability that one new patient adheres.

2.10 Counts: the Gamma–Poisson model
Counts with exposure \(E\) (patient-days, person-years): \(y \sim \text{Poisson}(E\lambda)\). With a \(\text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)\) prior (shape \(\alpha\), rate \(\beta\); mean \(\alpha/\beta\)):
\[\lambda \mid y \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha + y,\; \beta + E).\]
Add the count to the shape and the exposure to the rate. The prior behaves like \(\alpha\) events in \(\beta\) units of exposure.

Worked example: hospital-acquired infections. Rate \(\lambda\) per 1,000 patient-days. Similar wards have rates of roughly 1 to 9, around 4: prior Gamma(4, 1) (mean 4, 95% interval 1.1–8.8). A ward records 3 infections in 2,500 patient-days (\(E = 2.5\)), observed rate 1.2.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
text:
2.11 Unknown mean and variance
With both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) unknown you cannot multiply the two one-parameter conjugate priors: the posterior of \(\mu\) depends on \(\sigma\) and vice versa. They have a joint posterior, and the marginal posterior of \(\mu\) means integrating over \(\sigma\):
\[p(\mu \mid y) = \int p(\mu, \sigma \mid y)\, d\sigma.\]

The joint conjugate prior is the normal–inverse-Gamma: \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}\) and \(\mu \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma^2/\kappa_0)\). The prior for \(\mu\) is wider when \(\sigma^2\) is large: a funnel shape.
With the reference prior \(p(\mu, \sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2\) you get \(\dfrac{\mu - \bar y}{s/\sqrt n} \Bigm| y \sim t_{n-1}\): the classical t-interval, with a Bayesian reading. The t distribution appears because the uncertainty about σ has been integrated out.









Figure 3: Draws from a normal–inverse-Gamma distribution (left) and from independent priors with the same marginal for σ² (right). Log scale for the variance.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
section: 2.12 Linear models and the limits of conjugacy
text:
2.12 Linear models and the limits of conjugacy
The linear model \(y_i \sim N(\alpha + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dots + \beta_p x_{ip}, \sigma^2)\) needs priors for \(\alpha\), each \(\beta_j\) and \(\sigma\) (not for the \(\mu_i\), which are functions of the parameters). Notes on the joint posterior:

It is correlated: the intercept correlates with the slopes unless predictors are centred, and non-orthogonal designs correlate the slopes.
With flat priors on the coefficients and \(1/\sigma^2\) on the variance you recover OLS and its t and \(\chi^2\) results.
Informative priors make impossible OLS problems possible: with \(p + 1 \geq n\) or collinear predictors, OLS has no unique solution, but a proper prior regularises the problem (ridge regression is the classical analogue). The answer then depends strongly on the prior.

Where conjugacy ends. No conjugate prior exists for Student-t data (robust to outliers), for censored or left-truncated data (values below a detection limit), for logistic regression, or for most multi-parameter models. Grids fail beyond a few parameters. Module 3 solves this with MCMC.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
text:
When to use conjugate analysis

Single-parameter problems where the prior can be stated as a mean and a spread: proportions (Beta), rates (Gamma), means with known variance (normal).
Quick sanity checks and back-of-the-envelope updates, including checking MCMC output against an exact answer.
Explaining a Bayesian analysis to collaborators: “the prior is worth 20 patients”.
Sequential monitoring, where the posterior after each batch becomes the next prior.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
text:
Limitations

Only a short list of likelihood–prior pairs is conjugate. Choosing a prior family because it is conjugate is convenience, not knowledge; with enough data this rarely matters, with little data it can.
Several parameters with dependence need joint priors that are hard to specify and interpret.
Truncation, censoring, heavy tails and hierarchical structure all leave the conjugate world.

title: Module 2 — Continuous Priors: Conjugate Distributions
text:
Why-questions






NoteWhy does the posterior variance always shrink in the normal model, even when data and prior disagree?





Precisions add, and the data precision \(n/\sigma^2\) does not depend on where the data lie. In the Beta–Binomial model this is only approximately true: data near 0.5 can widen the posterior compared with a prior near 0 or 1, because the binomial variance \(\theta(1-\theta)\) depends on the value.









NoteWhy is shrinkage not “bias we should avoid”?





Shrinking towards the prior introduces bias for any individual whose true value is far from the prior mean, but it reduces variance. When many estimates are made (patients, hospitals, genes) the total error is usually smaller. This bias–variance trade-off is the core of Module 5.









NoteWhy is the t distribution a Bayesian result too?





It is the marginal posterior of μ after averaging over the uncertainty about σ. A normal distribution with σ plugged in would ignore that uncertainty and be too narrow, the same lesson as the plug-in predictive in Section 2.9.

The likelihood must be defined wherever the prior is positive, and some values with positive prior must give the observed data positive probability. (1.4)

title: Module 4 — Model Checks, Comparisons and Stacking
text:
After Module 3 you can fit a model and show that the MCMC converged. That only means you have an accurate picture of the posterior under the model you assumed. A badly wrong model converges just as happily as a good one. Module 4 asks the next questions: Is this model any good? Where does it fall short? Would another model do better?
The first tool is the posterior predictive check (PPC). Because Bayesian models are generative, you can simulate “replicated” datasets from the fitted model and compare them with the data you actually observed. If the replications systematically miss a feature you care about (the tails, the share of zeros, the pattern across subgroups), the model needs work.
The second tool estimates out-of-sample predictive performance. The ideal measure is the expected log predictive density for new data (elpd), rooted in the Kullback–Leibler divergence. AIC, DIC, WAIC and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) are increasingly good estimates of it. brms reports LOO with a standard error, so you can see whether a difference between models is larger than its uncertainty.
The third idea is stacking: rather than picking one model, average the predictive distributions of several, with weights chosen for predictive performance. The module ends by computing the actual target of inference, often a non-linear function of parameters, from the draws.

section: 4.3 Test statistics and posterior predictive p-values
text:
4.3 Test statistics and posterior predictive p-values
For a binary outcome, a density plot of zeros and ones says little. Choose a test statistic \(T(y)\) instead: the proportion of ones, the mean in a subgroup, the maximum, the share of zeros, a correlation between repeated measurements. Compute it for the data and for every replication:
\[p_\text{B} = P\big(T(y^\text{rep}) \geq T(y) \mid y\big) \approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_s I\big(T(y^{\text{rep}(s)}) \geq T(y)\big).\]

A value near 0.5 means the observed statistic sits in the middle of the replications: the model reproduces this feature.
Near 0 or 1 means the observed value is in a tail: the model misses this feature. The notes suggest treating values below about 0.11 or above 0.89 as a reason to extend the model (the threshold depends on how important the feature is).
Choose statistics that the model does not fit directly. A model with an intercept will always reproduce the overall mean, so checking the mean is weak. Check what the model does not explicitly fit: tails, subgroups, variables left out of the model, the dependence between repeated measurements.


  The overall proportion of ones
  The proportion of ones within each region
  The mean of the replicated proportion of ones
  The number of observations in each replication
  The intercept makes the model reproduce the overall proportion almost by construction. A grouping variable that is not in the model (region) is where systematic misfit can show up. The last two options are not checks of fit at all.







WarningCommon confusion: PPCs and multiple testing



Posterior predictive checks are not inferences about parameters or predictions of new data: they are diagnostics, like trace plots. The notes say there is no need to correct for multiple testing. Check as many features as are relevant, then act: extend the model, or report the limitation.

section: 4.6 Out-of-sample performance: KL divergence and elpd
text:
4.6 Out-of-sample performance: KL divergence and elpd
The objective way to judge a model is how well it predicts new data. The notes build the ideal measure from the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the true distribution of new data \(g\) and the model’s predictive distribution \(f\):
\[D_\text{KL}(g \,\|\, f) = \int g(\tilde y) \log\frac{g(\tilde y)}{f(\tilde y)}\,d\tilde y \;\geq 0, \qquad = 0 \text{ only if } f = g.\]

It is asymmetric: \(D_\text{KL}(g\|f) \neq D_\text{KL}(f\|g)\). A too-narrow prediction that misses where data actually land is punished more than a too-wide one (“the expected surprise” when reality turns out to be \(g\)).
When comparing models, \(\int g \log g\) is the same constant for all of them, so only \(E_g[\log f(\tilde y)]\) matters. Summed over observations this is the expected log pointwise predictive density:

\[\text{elpd} = \sum_{i=1}^n E_{g_i}\big[\log p(\tilde y_i \mid y)\big].\]
Higher elpd = better predictions. We never know \(g\), so every method below is an estimate of elpd.

text:
4.8 Leave-one-out cross-validation
Cross-validation estimates elpd directly: fit on part of the data, evaluate the log predictive density on the held-out part. No penalty is needed, because the test data were not used for fitting.

k-fold CV: split into \(k\) folds, fit \(k\) times. Each fit uses a fraction \((k-1)/k\) of the data.
LOO-CV: \(k = n\). Refitting \(n\) times is expensive, but PSIS-LOO (Pareto-smoothed importance sampling) approximates it from a single fit: loo(fit) in brms.
Pareto \(\hat k\) diagnostics. Each observation gets a \(\hat k\). Values below 0.7 are fine. Above 0.7, that observation is highly influential and the approximation is unreliable for it: use loo(fit, moment_match = TRUE) (the model must be fitted with save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)), loo(fit, reloo = TRUE), or kfold(fit, K = 10).

What does “leave one out” mean for your data? LOO answers “how well do I predict a new observation from a group I have already seen?” To predict a new group (a new hospital, region or country), leave out whole groups: kfold(fit, folds = "grouped", group = "hospital", K = 10). For time series, predict the future from the past. The notes recommend LOO-PSIS or k-fold over WAIC; LOO also gives the \(\hat k\) warnings that WAIC lacks.

  A predicts better, because its elpd_diff is negative
  The standard error is too large, so LOO has failed
  |−2.1| < 4 and about 1.2 SE: within the noise of the estimate. Report both, check whether they lead to the same conclusions, or stack them. A negative elpd_diff means worse than the top model.







WarningCommon confusion: model comparison as variable selection



Choosing variables by repeated model comparison is a data-driven search with the same multiple-testing problems as stepwise selection, and the chosen model’s intervals are too narrow. Use comparison to learn which features predict and which patterns a model misses; choose adjustment variables from subject-matter knowledge (confounders) instead.

title: Module 4 — Model Checks, Comparisons and Stacking
text:
4.10 Stacking and Bayesian model averaging
If several models predict reasonably well, a weighted average of their predictive distributions often predicts better than any single one, without fitting a new model:
\[p(\tilde y \mid y, \text{stack}) = \sum_j w_j\, p(\tilde y \mid y, \text{model}_j), \qquad w_j \geq 0,\; \sum_j w_j = 1.\]

WAIC or LOO weights (“pseudo-BMA”, as in the notes): \(w_j = \dfrac{\exp(-\tfrac12 \text{WAIC}_j)}{\sum_k \exp(-\tfrac12 \text{WAIC}_k)}\). A model a few WAIC units worse gets a small weight; one much better gets nearly all.
Stacking weights: choose \(w\) to maximise the LOO predictive density of the mixture. Models that are good in different regions of the data both get weight.
In brms: loo_model_weights(list(a = loo_a, b = loo_b), method = "stacking") or "pseudobma"; pp_average(fit_a, fit_b) gives the averaged predictions.
Sampling from the stack: take \(w_j \times S\) draws from model \(j\)’s posterior predictive, then combine.

Why it helps. Two models that err in opposite directions in some region cancel part of each other’s error. If one model is better everywhere, it gets (nearly) all the weight and stacking changes nothing.
Caution. Stacking is for prediction. Averaging a parameter across models is often meaningless, because “the coefficient of x” means something different when the other covariates differ.

Limitations

PPCs use the data twice (to fit and to check), so they are conservative: they find gross misfit more easily than subtle misfit. p-values near 0.5 do not prove the model right.
LOO estimates prediction for data like yours. It cannot detect confounding, and a model with better predictions is not necessarily the right causal model.
LOO is unreliable with many high Pareto \(\hat k\) values (small clusters, very flexible models); use k-fold CV then.
Information criteria compare models on the same outcome. They cannot compare models fitted to different datasets or different transformations without adjustment.

Which statistics does model A fail? What share of model A’s replicated stays are negative (mean(yrep_A < 0))?
Invent a statistic that model B might fail, for example the share of stays longer than 14 days. Check it.







TipModel answer






Model A fails the minimum (p ≈ 0.001: replicated minima are almost always below the observed 1.1 days, usually negative) and skewness (p ≈ 0: the data are right-skewed, the normal is symmetric). The maximum is borderline (p ≈ 0.07). About 7% of replicated stays are negative, which is impossible. Model B’s p-values are all between 0.3 and 0.8.
ppp(yrep_B, function(y) mean(y > 14)) is around 0.5. Model B passes, as it should, since these data were simulated from a log-normal. With real data, look for features that matter clinically: the share of very long stays drives bed planning.

Interpret the difference using the rules of thumb from Section 4.9.
Why are the weights so extreme?
Why would comparing dnorm(log(y), ...) for model B with dnorm(y, ...) for model A be wrong?







TipModel answer






Model B’s elpd is about 20 higher, with an SE of the difference of about 5: more than 4 and about 4 SE. A clear predictive advantage for the log-normal.

In RStudio: brms tasks






ImportantHow the RStudio tasks work



Each task simulates its own data. Try first, then open the solution. The solutions were run with brms 2.23; your numbers will differ slightly. Download all Module 4 tasks: module4-tasks.R.



Task 4.1 · Normal or Student-t for sodium readings with some faulty values
set.seed(520)
bad_reading <- rbinom(300, size = 1, prob = 0.05)
sodium <- data.frame(value = ifelse(bad_reading == 1,
                                    rnorm(300, mean = 140, sd = 15),
                                    rnorm(300, mean = 140, sd = 3)))

Fit value ~ 1 with family = gaussian() and with family = student() (priors: Intercept normal(140, 10), sigma exponential(0.2), nu gamma(2, 0.1)). Do both converge?
Compare pp_check(fit, ndraws = 50) for the two models.
Define share_near <- function(y) mean(abs(y - 140) < 3) and share_extreme <- function(y) mean(abs(y - 140) > 15). Use pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "share_near") and compute the posterior predictive p-values by hand.
Compare the models with loo_compare().







TipSolution





fit_normal <- brm(value ~ 1, family = gaussian(),
                  prior = c(prior(normal(140, 10), class = "Intercept"),
                            prior(exponential(0.2), class = "sigma")),
                  data = sodium, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 520, refresh = 0)
fit_student <- brm(value ~ 1, family = student(),
                   prior = c(prior(normal(140, 10), class = "Intercept"),
                             prior(exponential(0.2), class = "sigma"),
                             prior(gamma(2, 0.1), class = "nu")),
                   data = sodium, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 520, refresh = 0)
pp_check(fit_normal, ndraws = 50) + xlim(110, 170)
pp_check(fit_student, ndraws = 50) + xlim(110, 170)

yrep_normal  <- posterior_predict(fit_normal)
yrep_student <- posterior_predict(fit_student)
mean(apply(yrep_normal, 1, share_near) >= share_near(sodium$value))
mean(apply(yrep_student, 1, share_near) >= share_near(sodium$value))
# ... and the same for share_extreme
loo_compare(loo(fit_normal), loo(fit_student))
What we got: both converge (Rhat 1.00, ESS > 2,000). Normal: mean 140.08, sigma 4.79, inflated by the faulty readings (the good readings have SD 3). Student-t: mean 139.79, sigma 2.96, nu 3.7 (heavy tails).
Test statistics. Observed: 59.7% of readings lie within 3 mmol/L of 140, and 1.7% lie more than 15 away.

Task 4.2 · A binary outcome: flu vaccination by age
set.seed(521)
vaccine <- data.frame(age = round(runif(800, min = 20, max = 85)))
true_logodds <- -1.2 + 0.0008 * (vaccine$age - 20)^2       # uptake accelerates with age
vaccine$vaccinated <- rbinom(800, size = 1, prob = plogis(true_logodds))
vaccine$age10 <- (vaccine$age - 50) / 10
vaccine$age_group <- cut(vaccine$age, breaks = c(19, 35, 50, 65, 75, 85))

Fit vaccinated ~ age10 (family = bernoulli(), priors normal(0, 1.5) Intercept and normal(0, 1) b). Check pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "mean"). Is that a useful check?

Note: pp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", group = "age_group") stops with “Variable ‘age_group’ could not be found in the data”: brms only accepts grouping variables that are in the model, even with newdata. fit_linear <- brm(vaccinated ~ age10, family = bernoulli(),
                  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
                            prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b")),
                  data = vaccine, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 521, refresh = 0)

                     prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
                               prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b")),
                     data = vaccine, chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 521, refresh = 0)
pp_check(fit_linear, type = "stat", stat = "mean")

yrep_linear    <- posterior_predict(fit_linear)
yrep_quadratic <- posterior_predict(fit_quadratic)
bayesplot::ppc_stat_grouped(y = vaccine$vaccinated, yrep = yrep_linear,
                            group = vaccine$age_group, stat = "mean")

Using the two LOO objects from Task 4.2, compute loo_model_weights(..., method = "stacking") and method = "pseudobma". Do the two methods agree? When would they differ?

Task 4.4 · The estimand: how much more likely is a 70-year-old to be vaccinated than a 40-year-old?
Using the quadratic model, compute the posterior of the risk difference \(P(\text{vaccinated} \mid 70) - P(\text{vaccinated} \mid 40)\) with posterior_epred(). Report the median, a 95% interval and \(P(\text{difference} > 0.3)\).






TipSolution





ages_of_interest <- data.frame(age10 = c((40 - 50) / 10, (70 - 50) / 10))
risk_draws <- posterior_epred(fit_quadratic, newdata = ages_of_interest)   # draws x 2
risk_difference <- risk_draws[, 2] - risk_draws[, 1]
quantile(risk_difference, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
mean(risk_difference > 0.3)
What we got: median risk difference 0.40, 95% credible interval 0.33 to 0.46, and \(P(\text{difference} > 0.3 \mid y) \approx 0.999\). A 70-year-old is about 40 percentage points more likely to be vaccinated than a 40-year-old. That sentence answers the question directly, which a log-odds coefficient for age10 and another for its square do not.

title: Module 4 — Model Checks, Comparisons and Stacking
text:
Why-questions






NoteWhy check features the model does not fit directly?





A model reproduces what it was built to reproduce: an intercept guarantees the overall mean, a group term guarantees the group means. Misfit shows up in features that were not built in: tails, subgroups, dependence, variables left out.









NoteWhy does WAIC need a penalty but cross-validation does not?





WAIC evaluates the model on the same data used to fit it, which is optimistic; the penalty corrects for that optimism. Cross-validation evaluates on held-out data, so there is no optimism to correct (only a small pessimism, because each fit uses fewer observations).









NoteWhy is the standard error of an elpd difference smaller than the two separate standard errors suggest?





Both models are evaluated on the same observations, so their pointwise elpd values are strongly correlated. The paired SE uses the variance of the pointwise differences, which removes the shared variation between observations.

Spaced review: Modules 1–3






Note1. What is the difference between posterior_epred and posterior_predict?





epred: draws of the expected outcome (the mean, a probability). predict: draws of a new observation, which adds the outcome’s own randomness. (3.12)









Note2. Your summary shows Rhat 1.00 but 50 divergent transitions. Can you trust it?





Not yet. Divergences mean the sampler may have missed a region of the posterior, so estimates may be biased. Increase adapt_delta, and consider reparameterising or tighter priors. (3.7)









Note3. Why does a Beta(1, 1) prior give credible intervals with roughly nominal coverage?





It adds no information, so the posterior is driven by the likelihood like a classical interval. Priors centred away from the truth under-cover. (2.8)

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
text:
Module 1 described the Bayesian analysis in four tidy steps: model, prior, posterior, evaluation. Real analyses never run in a straight line. A posterior predictive check fails and you change the likelihood; the chains do not converge and you simplify the model or tighten a prior; a prior predictive check shows the prior allows absurd data and you rethink it. Module 6 is about doing this loop well and honestly. It is also the blueprint for your project.
The main new tool is the prior predictive check: simulate data from the prior alone, before looking at the data, and see whether the prior implies plausible outcomes. It is the easiest way to make sense of priors in many dimensions, where the joint effect of individually “vague” priors can be surprisingly extreme, especially through a link function.
The module then turns to open problems. Every time the data make you change the model or the prior, you use the data twice, which breaks temporal coherence. What counts as a “good” prior: one with good frequentist properties (calibration), one with mathematical invariance (Jeffreys, reference priors), or one that honestly encodes expert knowledge? And is Bayesian statistics more “subjective” than classical statistics? The syllabus asks you to discuss these questions, so there is no single right answer to memorise. The aim is a defensible position.

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
text:
6.1 The workflow is iterative
The four steps from Module 1, with the loops that real analyses need:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Model: likelihood + structure for everything (data, θ)   │◀──────────┐
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘           │
  ┌──────────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐           │
  │ 2. Prior ── prior predictive check ── absurd? change prior ─┼──┐        │
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘  │ still  │
  ┌──────────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐  │ absurd?│
  │ 3. Fit: MCMC ── converged? (R-hat, ESS, divergences) ── no ─┼──┴────────┤
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘           │
  ┌──────────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐           │
  │ 4. Check: posterior predictive checks, LOO ── misfit? ──────┼───────────┘
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐
  │ 5. Several plausible models? compare, stack, or report all  │
  │ 6. Sensitivity: priors, model choices                        │
  │ 7. Estimands from the draws → tables, figures, conclusions   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Gelman et al. (2020) list many more steps, including “add more data” and “give up”: not every question can be answered with the data at hand. Two practical habits make the loop manageable:

Start simple and build up: an intercept-only model, then covariates, then group effects, then varying slopes. When something breaks, you know which addition broke it.
Keep a log of every model you fit and why you changed it. You need it for the methods section anyway (Section 6.3).

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
text:
6.2 Prior predictive checks
Simulate data from the prior alone: draw parameters from the prior, plug them into the likelihood, look at the simulated outcomes. In brms, add sample_prior = "only" to brm(), then use pp_check() and posterior_predict() exactly as for the posterior.
What to look for:

The prior predictive should cover every outcome that is plausible: previously observed ranges, theoretically possible values.
It should not put much mass on implausible outcomes: negative lengths of stay, blood pressures of 900, a 100% or 0% prevalence in every population.
It is not supposed to reproduce your data. That would mean you tuned the prior on the data (Section 6.3).









Figure 1: Implied probability of vaccination at age 20 under two priors for a logistic regression (intercept and slope per decade, age centred at 50). Each histogram shows 4,000 prior draws.





The “vague” prior is not vague at all on the probability scale: it says almost every 20-year-old population is either nearly all vaccinated or nearly all unvaccinated (the U shape). Priors that look weak on the linear-predictor scale can be strongly informative on the outcome scale once they pass through a link function or are combined across many coefficients.






WarningCommon confusion: “a flat or very wide prior is the safe, neutral choice”



A flat prior on a coefficient says an odds ratio of \(10^6\) is as plausible as 1.5. Flat priors can also give improper posteriors or poor convergence. A weakly informative prior that rules out absurd values is usually safer. A prior predictive check shows what each prior actually implies.



  Nothing, since priors should always be vague
  Tighten or rescale the priors until simulated weights are plausible
  Tune the prior until it reproduces the observed weights exactly
  Switch to a flat prior, which cannot produce impossible values
  The prior implies impossible data, so revise it (or the likelihood, e.g. a log-normal for a positive outcome). Tuning the prior to reproduce the observed data uses the data twice. A flat prior makes the problem worse.

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
section: 6.3 Temporal coherence: using the data twice
text:
6.3 Temporal coherence: using the data twice
Strict Bayesian updating says: specify the prior before seeing the data, and never revisit it. Every time a check on the data makes you widen a prior or add a term, the “prior” of the final model has been informed by the data, which is then used again to compute the posterior. The notes (following David Cox) call this a loss of temporal coherence.

Changing the model after a failed posterior predictive check is equivalent to changing the prior on an extra coefficient from “exactly zero” to something weaker, using the data.
It is not a Bayesian problem only: stepwise variable selection, choosing among many models, and choosing covariates after looking at results all make classical p-values and intervals too optimistic.
It is not a reason to keep a model you know is wrong. Cox: hypotheses generated by the data are not worthless, but they are “in some way distinct from hypotheses considered a priori”, and cannot be trusted as much as a test on fresh data.

What to do in practice:

Plan as much as possible before looking at outcomes: research question, estimand, model family, priors, planned checks. For found data (like survey data) this is harder but still possible.
Report every model fitted and every change made, and why.
Temper your conclusions for data-driven choices; present them as hypotheses for new data.

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
text:
6.5 Prior sensitivity analysis
Show how much the conclusions depend on the priors:

Fit the main analysis with your chosen priors.
Refit with alternatives: wider, narrower, differently centred (for example a sceptical prior centred on no effect), a different family for SDs.
Report the estimand under each. If the conclusions agree, say so. If they do not, the data alone cannot settle the question, and that is a finding to report.

Most informative are priors for parameters the data say little about: group-level SDs with few groups, coefficients of rare exposures, interactions. The same logic applies to model choices: normal vs Student-t, with or without a random slope. The priorsense package (power-scaling sensitivity) automates part of this for brms fits.
Compare prior and posterior for key parameters: a posterior identical to the prior means the data are uninformative about that parameter.

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
section: 6.6 Calibration: frequentist properties of Bayesian procedures
text:
6.6 Calibration: frequentist properties of Bayesian procedures
How good is a prior? Borrow classical criteria (bias, coverage, efficiency) and study them by simulation:

Choose a data-generating mechanism and true parameter values (several settings, some unfavourable).
Simulate many datasets; fit the model with the chosen prior to each.
Record bias of the posterior mean, coverage of the credible intervals, and interval width.

What to expect: a prior centred on the truth over-covers; one centred ±2 prior SDs away under-covers (2.8). A reasonable hope is good coverage on average over plausible true values.
Simulation-based calibration (SBC). Draw the true value from the prior itself, simulate data, fit, and compute where the true value falls in its posterior (its posterior quantile). If model, prior and software are all correct, these quantiles are uniform and the 95% intervals cover 95% of the time on average. Stan’s developers use this to test the software. A non-uniform histogram reveals a bug or a mismatch between the prior used for generating and for fitting.
crumbs: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
text:
6.7 “Objective” priors
Attempts to define priors by mathematical principle rather than knowledge:

Flat priors. Not invariant: flat on \(\sigma\) is not flat on \(\sigma^2\) or \(\log\sigma\). If \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(7, 22)\), then \(X^2\) is not uniform on \((49, 484)\).
Jeffreys’ prior, \(p(\theta) \propto \sqrt{I(\theta)}\) (Fisher information). Invariant under reparameterisation: you get the same answer whether you work with \(\theta\) or \(\theta^2\). Examples: flat for a normal mean with known variance; \(\text{Beta}(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) for a binomial proportion; \(1/\sigma\) for a normal SD. Critiques: depends on the likelihood (so two analysts with different models get different “non-informative” priors), and multi-parameter versions are controversial.
Reference priors maximise the expected KL divergence between prior and posterior: they let the data dominate as much as possible. In one dimension they usually coincide with Jeffreys’.
Priors that mimic frequentist results (probability matching), shrinkage priors for sparsity (spike-and-slab, horseshoe), and penalised complexity (PC) priors that favour the simpler model. These are active research areas.

None has settled the question: “objective” priors are conventions that other analysts can reproduce.
crumbs: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
section: 6.8 Subjectivity in Bayesian and non-Bayesian workflows
text:
6.8 Subjectivity in Bayesian and non-Bayesian workflows
The syllabus asks you to discuss subjectivity in data collection, prior specification and model specification. The notes’ main points:

Every analysis is full of choices: research question, data source, inclusion criteria, variables, model family, functional form, how to handle outliers and missing data, what to report. In a classical analysis many of these are implicit. Choosing not to use a prior is also a choice.
The prior is often the least dangerous choice: it is explicit, can be checked with prior predictive checks and varied in a sensitivity analysis. Its influence fades with more data (though not with more parameters: in genomics, with many small clusters or with \(p \gg n\), priors stay influential).
Informative priors can be more accurate. The German tank problem in Module 1 of the notes and the fish example in Module 1 here: a well-reasoned prior plus little data beats little data alone.
“Objective” may really mean transparent and reproducible: report every step so others could reproduce it or vary it (Draper’s “transparent subjectivity”).
Eliciting priors from experts is a skill. Experts’ priors disagree, are often overconfident, and eliciting them costs time; facilitation protocols exist. In practice defaults and weakly informative priors fill the gap.
The statistician’s role. Priors are where domain experts can contribute directly without knowing MCMC. The notes imagine collaborators debating priors and predictive checks instead of p-values.







NoteDiscussion prompts for the seminar or the project report






Name three subjective choices in a classical analysis of your project data that a reader might not notice.
Your collaborator says “Bayesian results are just your opinion”. Give a two-sentence reply using the fish example or a sensitivity analysis.
When would you prefer a sceptical prior over a weakly informative one? Who should decide?
You changed the model after a failed posterior predictive check. How do you report that honestly?

When to use these tools

Prior predictive checks: for every model with non-trivial priors, especially GLMs and GLMMs where link functions distort vague priors.
Sensitivity analysis: for every published analysis; essential for group-level SDs with few groups and for parameters the data barely inform.
Calibration / SBC: when you write a new model or custom Stan code, or want to know how a prior behaves under repeated use.

title: Module 6 — Bayesian Workflow and Open Problems
text:
Limitations

Prior predictive checks only reveal absurd marginal implications that you think to look at; a prior can pass them and still be poor.
Sensitivity analyses can only vary what you think of varying.
There is no agreed definition of an “objective” prior, and a fully coherent workflow is rarely achievable with found data.

Exercise 1 · A prior predictive check by hand. Logistic regression for vaccination by age (age in decades from 50).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Why is the share of extreme probabilities lower at age 50 than at ages 20 and 80?
Try implied_probabilities(1.5, 0.5). Is a slope SD of 0.5 per decade reasonable for vaccination uptake?







TipModel answer






At age 50, age10 = 0, so only the intercept matters. At 20 and 80 the slope is multiplied by ±3, so its prior spread is tripled on the log-odds scale. With the wide prior about 88% of draws are extreme at ages 20 and 80, and still 65% at age 50.
SD 0.5 per decade means an odds ratio per decade mostly between \(e^{-1} \approx 0.37\) and \(e^{1} \approx 2.7\), and across 30 years between about 0.05 and 20. Plausible for uptake that rises strongly with age, without absurd values. Whether it is “right” is a subject-matter question.




Exercise 2 · Simulation-based calibration of a Beta–Binomial model.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Explain the shape of the second histogram. In which direction are the posteriors wrong?
Fit with a flat prior (a_fit = 1, b_fit = 1) while generating from Beta(2, 2). Is it calibrated? Why is that not a contradiction?







TipModel answer






Most true values fall in the lowest part of their posteriors: the Beta(8, 2) prior pulls every posterior upwards, so the truth sits in the lower tail. Coverage drops to about 0.71 instead of 0.95.
Close to uniform, coverage about 0.95. With 20 observations the flat prior lets the data dominate, and it does not pull in a systematically wrong direction. Calibration “on average” does not require the fitting prior to equal the generating one, but mismatch in location, as in Question 3, shows up quickly.

text:
In RStudio: brms tasks






ImportantHow the RStudio tasks work



The data are simulated in the script (the same vaccination data as Task 4.2). Download: module6-tasks.R.



Task 6.1 · Prior predictive check with sample_prior = "only"
Fit vaccinated ~ age10 twice with sample_prior = "only": once with normal(0, 10) on both intercept and slope, once with normal(0, 1.5) (Intercept) and normal(0, 1) (b).

Compare pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "mean") for the two priors.
What share of prior draws implies an overall vaccination share below 5% or above 95%?
What share of prior draws implies a probability below 1% at age 20?







TipSolution





prior_wide <- brm(vaccinated ~ age10, family = bernoulli(),
                  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 10), class = "Intercept"),
                            prior(normal(0, 10), class = "b")),
                  data = vaccine, sample_prior = "only",
                  chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 610, refresh = 0)
prior_weak <- brm(vaccinated ~ age10, family = bernoulli(),
                  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
                            prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b")),
                  data = vaccine, sample_prior = "only",
                  chains = 4, iter = 1000, seed = 610, refresh = 0)
pp_check(prior_wide, type = "stat", stat = "mean")
pp_check(prior_weak, type = "stat", stat = "mean")

prior_share_wide <- rowMeans(posterior_predict(prior_wide))
prior_share_weak <- rowMeans(posterior_predict(prior_weak))
c(mean(prior_share_wide < 0.05 | prior_share_wide > 0.95),
  mean(prior_share_weak < 0.05 | prior_share_weak > 0.95))

extreme_ages <- data.frame(age10 = c(-3, 3))
c(mean(posterior_epred(prior_wide, newdata = extreme_ages)[, 1] < 0.01),
  mean(posterior_epred(prior_weak, newdata = extreme_ages)[, 1] < 0.01))
What we got: the overall share looks less alarming than you might expect: 19% of the wide-prior draws imply an overall vaccination share below 5% or above 95%, against 2% for the weak prior. With a steep prior slope, young people end up near 0 and old people near 1, so the average lands in the middle. The overall mean hides the problem, and brms even warns that “mean” is a weak statistic.
At a specific age the difference is stark: 47% of wide-prior draws put the probability of vaccination at age 20 below 1%, against 11% for the weak prior. Check prior implications at the covariate values that matter, not only overall.





Task 6.2 · Prior sensitivity: does the conclusion change?
Refit both models to the data (update(prior_weak, sample_prior = "no")) and compare the posterior of the age slope. What does the comparison tell you, and when would you expect a larger difference?






TipSolution





fit_weak <- update(prior_weak, sample_prior = "no", seed = 611, refresh = 0)
fit_wide <- update(prior_wide, sample_prior = "no", seed = 611, refresh = 0)
rbind(weak = posterior_summary(fit_weak, variable = "b_age10"),
      wide = posterior_summary(fit_wide, variable = "b_age10"))
What we got: b_age10 = 0.503 (SD 0.044) with the weak prior and 0.505 (SD 0.045) with the wide prior. Practically identical: 800 people inform one slope far more than either prior does.
Expect priors to matter more with few observations or few events, group-level SDs with few groups (Task 5.5), many coefficients relative to the data, and separation (a covariate predicts the outcome perfectly, so the likelihood keeps increasing towards infinite coefficients and only the prior stops it). A prior predictive check is worth doing even when the posterior turns out insensitive, because you do not know in advance which case you are in.

text:
Why-questions






NoteWhy check the prior on the outcome scale rather than the parameter scale?





Priors on individual parameters combine (and pass through link functions) in ways that are hard to foresee. The outcome scale is where domain knowledge lives: experts know plausible blood pressures and prevalences, not plausible log odds ratios.









NoteWhy is revising a model after a failed check still better than keeping it?





A model known to be wrong gives conclusions known to be unreliable. Revising uses the data twice, which makes the final uncertainty somewhat optimistic; reporting the revision lets readers judge that.









NoteWhy doesn’t more data make priors irrelevant in hierarchical models?





Adding observations within existing groups sharpens each group’s estimate, but τ is informed by the number of groups. More groups add parameters too, so the ratio of parameters to data does not go to zero, and priors on group-level quantities stay influential.

Note1. What does a posterior predictive p-value of 0.98 for the maximum mean?





Replicated maxima are almost always larger than the observed maximum: the model predicts heavier upper tails than the data show. (4.3)









Note2. Why is a new group’s prediction wider than an existing group’s?





It adds a draw of the group effect from N(0, τ²), with τ itself uncertain; an existing group’s effect is informed by its own data. (5.6)
